a_rows_sample.statement: S2226's refusal of v_{t+1}>v_t ('higher is not always better': uncertainty may decrease, provenance completeness may increase, contradiction may decrease) is formally a Pareto-dominance problem: K_{t+1} succeq_Pareto K_t iff for all dimensions d, v_{t+1}(d) is no worse, and for some d, strictly better -- a Pareto order is a partial order admitting incomparable states by construction. Identified as the FIFTH independent route (of five distinct methods: Sigma-axis-order measurement per Step 291 finding 0 of 5 axes ordered; retraction non-monotonicity per Step 288/06; two separate corpus refusals to claim a semilattice, Steps 060 sec60.71 and 061/274.32; and now this Pareto argument) all converging on: there is no total order on K -- assessed as among the best-supported negative results in the programme.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Moksha \sim transcendence of the conditioning regime ... G_t\rightarrow G_{\perp}
a_rows_sample.statement: Revises the earlier Moksha formulation (Delta_t -> 0) given Chapter 14: Moksha != maximum K and Moksha != maximum Sattva; instead Moksha ~ transcendence of the conditioning regime, formalized as the research placeholder G_t -> G_perp meaning 'outside the three-mode conditioning model' -- explicitly flagged as a KnowledgeOS mathematical placeholder, not a Gita term. Proposes a purification trajectory Tamas-dominant -> (discrimination/clarification) -> Rajas-dominant -> (disciplined activity) -> Sattva-dominant -> (transcendence) -> Guna-atita, and a candidate epistemic-state model E_t=(K_t,Sigma_t,G_t,N_t) with N_t -Buddhi-> o_t and K_{t+1}=delta(K_t,o_t).

a_rows_sample.anchor: \Delta\text{Knowledge} = \Delta\text{Dimension} + \Delta\text{Quality} ... Knowledge Growth requires Discrimination
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes dimension from value: a statement could add a new dimension but have poor epistemic quality, or add no new dimension yet dramatically improve reliability/consistency/provenance/resolution/confidence/contextual understanding -- decomposed (as a research decomposition only) as Delta Knowledge = Delta Dimension + Delta Quality. Argues K_{t+1}>K_t in quantity does not imply K_{t+1} succ K_t epistemically, because more information != better knowledge; the kernel therefore requires Buddhi to discriminate: Knowledge Growth requires Discrimination, not merely ingestion.

a_rows_sample.anchor: M\neq K_{\max} ... M\neq |\mathcal K|\rightarrow\infty ... M\sim\text{transformation of the relationship between Knower, Field and Horizon}
a_rows_sample.statement: With Chapters 11-14 combined, refuses modeling Moksha as the final Knowledge State: M != K_max and M != |K|->infinity. Proposes instead M ~ transformation of the relationship between Knower, Field and Horizon, combined with Chapter 14's transcendence of ordinary conditioning; the theoretical transition is not simply K_0->K_1->K_2->... but (N,K_t,rho_t,G_t,Omega) -> different epistemic regime.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge quantity \neq Knowledge quality ... Purification \neq accumulation
a_rows_sample.statement: Refines purification: P:Sigma_t->Sigma_{t+1} must not assume P(Sigma_t)>Sigma_t (per Step 287's finding that axes lack fully declared orders); instead a desired property Q(Sigma_{t+1})>=Q(Sigma_t) is wanted where Q is a future epistemic-quality functional that does not yet exist (an important research gap). Illustrates via example that K_1={1000 unsupported claims} could contain more information than K_2={100 well-supported claims} yet K_2 may be epistemically superior -- so Knowledge quantity != Knowledge quality, and Purification != accumulation; the kernel should maximize epistemic adequacy, not raw knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: confidence: 0.9\rightarrow0.4 could actually represent epistemic improvement ... Purification \neq monotonic increase of every metric
a_rows_sample.statement: Sharpens the non-monotonicity of purification with a concrete numeric example: confidence going from 0.9 to 0.4 could represent epistemic improvement if new evidence shows the previous certainty was unjustified. Hence Purification != monotonic increase of every metric; Purification = progress toward a better-qualified epistemic state. Proposes P(K_t,E_t,B_t)=K_{t+1} performing: remove unsupported claims, resolve contradictions, separate observation from interpretation, identify missing evidence, reduce unjustified certainty, preserve provenance, incorporate valid new evidence, identify new dimensions. Also defines a transformation-quality functional Q_B(K_t,K_{t+1}) assessing whether a transition reduces contradiction, reduces unsupported assertions, makes uncertainty explicit, improves provenance, increases justified knowledge, detects hidden gaps, or avoids introducing unsupported claims -- assessed as more promising than trying to mathematically encode 'good' and 'evil'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge growth ... Knowledge expansion ... Knowledge purification ... These are not equivalent.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicitly rejects Purification=increase-in-dimensions-and-values as the canonical mathematical definition (confidence 0.95->0.55 can represent improvement if the original confidence was unjustified): Purification != monotonic increase; P(K_t,K_{t+1}) = improvement in epistemic quality, with quality itself still needing formal definition. Distinguishes three non-equivalent concepts: Knowledge growth (K_t->K_{t+1}, a state change occurs); Knowledge expansion (dim(K_{t+1})>dim(K_t), new dimensions represented); Knowledge purification (P(K_t,K_{t+1})=true, epistemic quality improves) -- more information does not imply better knowledge, and knowledge expansion != knowledge purification, assessed as an important theoretical safeguard. Also reformulates purification against Sigma as Sigma_t --B,Q,delta--> Sigma_{t+1} with P(Sigma_t,Sigma_{t+1}) rather than a scalar purity score, given Step 287's problem with total ordering.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Purification \approx reduction of epistemic distortion ... K_{t+1}\not\supseteq K_t does not imply deterioration.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects purification=increasing knowledge dimensions/values as the primary definition; proposes Purification ~ reduction of epistemic distortion, not more information. Example: K_t with P=verified becomes K_{t+1} with P=uncertain because new evidence shows the prior verification was inadequate -- numerically less certainty, epistemically better. Hence K_{t+1} not-superset-or-equal K_t does not imply deterioration.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Q(K_{t+1}) > Q(K_t) ... 100 pieces of noisy knowledge \downarrow purification \downarrow 20 pieces of highly qualified knowledge
a_rows_sample.statement: From 5.11 (purification through disciplined action without attachment): sharpens purification from |K_{t+1}|>|K_t| to Q(K_{t+1})>Q(K_t) where Q is a future epistemic-quality function. Concrete illustration: a kernel could transform 100 pieces of noisy knowledge into 20 pieces of highly qualified knowledge, becoming better despite becoming smaller -- assessed as a major correction to a purely information-quantity model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: J_t = w_A A_t+ w_S S_t+ w_R R_t+ w_V V_t+ w_C C_t - \lambda Z_t - \mu U_t
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes, explicitly non-canonical/for research purposes only, a candidate kernel objective function J_t = w_A A_t + w_S S_t + w_R R_t + w_V V_t + w_C C_t - lambda Z_t - mu U_t (weighted five Sigma axes minus unresolved-gap term Z minus unjustified-commitment term U), with purification meaning J_{t+1}>J_t -- explicitly not adopted because the measurement scales and per-axis ordering remain unresolved (per Step 287). Proposes Moksha as the limiting condition where repeated purification cycles reach Delta J -> 0 (the kernel can no longer improve the state under the available epistemic horizon) -- a philosophical hypothesis, not an architecture decision.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K_{t+1} \succeq_{Pareto} K_t \iff \forall d:\ v_{t+1}(d) \text{ no worse} \ \wedge\ \exists d:\ \text{strictly better}
b_rows_sample.statement: S2226's refusal of v_{t+1}>v_t ('higher is not always better': uncertainty may decrease, provenance completeness may increase, contradiction may decrease) is formally a Pareto-dominance problem: K_{t+1} succeq_Pareto K_t iff for all dimensions d, v_{t+1}(d) is no worse, and for some d, strictly better -- a Pareto order is a partial order admitting incomparable states by construction. Identified as the FIFTH independent route (of five distinct methods: Sigma-axis-order measurement per Step 291 finding 0 of 5 axes ordered; retraction non-monotonicity per Step 288/06; two separate corpus refusals to claim a semilattice, Steps 060 sec60.71 and 061/274.32; and now this Pareto argument) all converging on: there is no total order on K -- assessed as among the best-supported negative results in the programme.

b_rows_sample.anchor: M-Q3 and M-Q4 are ONE decision seen twice
b_rows_sample.statement: Sharpens gap M-Q3 (missing metric): the gap is not merely 'we lack a number' but that the dimensions are heterogeneous and their improvement directions differ, so no scalar metric can exist without a normative weighting -- and a weighting is a normative act, which is exactly gap M-Q4 (the undeclared loss function). Concludes M-Q3 and M-Q4 are the same decision seen twice, merged as M-Q3prime, a fact neither artifact 17 nor Step 291 had noticed.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \equiv_D \textbf{ silently presupposes a } dimension \textbf{ object.} The ratified eight carry Proposition, but neither dimension nor value.
b_rows_sample.statement: S2228's three-way sentence/proposition/dimension/value separation exposes a presupposition inside the ratified result equiv_D (264.15, value-level semantic equality: 3m not-equiv_str 300cm but 3m equiv_D 300cm) -- this comparison is only possible if a dimension (here, length) is fixed; without d, equiv_D has nothing to quantify over. The ratified eight primitives carry Proposition but neither dimension nor value, though equiv_D operates on the latter. Registered as D-Q1 with two open readings: (a) dimension/value are derived structure inside Proposition, so equiv_D is well-founded and the gap is merely documentary (assessed as the cheaper reading, not derived here); (b) they are missing primitives, which would contradict C-022's '50 attack classes, no counterexample' completeness claim. Also notes tension with Step 291's Audit A, which rates equiv_D Level-5 decidable 'but at the wrong level' -- this finding says the wrong level has no carrier at all, not merely irrelevance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: An open-ended tuple is the strongest form of the move `258.35` forbids.
b_rows_sample.statement: S2226's proposal K_t=(D_t,V_t,R_t,P_t,...) makes the dimension set itself time-indexed (D_t->D_{t+1}, discovery, alongside v_t(d)->v_{t+1}(d), improvement) -- genuinely new relative to Sigma's five fixed axes, since a state whose dimensional structure can grow is a different object. But it is an open-ended tuple, and Step 258.35 states K should be defined extensionally through behavioral sufficiency, not compositionally through an arbitrary tuple; an open-ended tuple is assessed as the strongest form of the move 258.35 forbids. Registered as D-Q2 (technically open, in tension with 258.35); tier T2, not promoted.

b_rows_sample.anchor: SIX disjoint operation vocabularies in the estate
b_rows_sample.statement: Counts six disjoint operation vocabularies now in the estate: (1) 272A's O_sem, 19 operations; (2) external_research pseudo-algorithm, 43 functions; (3) the corpus registry (256.2/259.7/261.19), 22 operations; (4) Ch13's type ontology, 7 (primitives not operations); (5) Omega_K={Discriminate,Qualify,Transition} + 11 named (artifact 20); (6, new, this batch) {E,R,C,X,Q,Z} from S2226 -- registered as G-91 (was three vocabularies at G-68, four at G-86, now six). Notes Qualify appears in both the fifth and sixth vocabularies (G-92): two independently constructed minimal-ish algebras both contain the one irreducible gap, reinforcing artifact 20's finding that any minimal kernel algebra containing Qualify inherits G1. Also notes both new sources ask about closure/associativity/non-commutativity, matching the corpus's own prior non-law (25J.46: 'we should not yet impose universal commutativity').

b_rows_sample.anchor: C8:\ \textbf{Purification} \neq \textbf{monotonic accumulation}
b_rows_sample.statement: Registers eighth negative constraint C8: Purification != monotonic accumulation ('higher is not always better'), joining C1-C7. Also records new T0: sentence=dimension, refused by its own source (S2228). Updated tally: T4 KERNEL stays 3, T4-SHAPE stays 1, T3 10->11, T2 10->13, T1 ~33->~34, T0 14->15; still zero new primitives, zero new canonical relations. Explicitly does not license: the Pareto finding does not supply an order (only explains why none exists, and that the missing piece is a normative weighting); the dimension/value layer is not promoted (D-Q1 unresolved); the sixth vocabulary is not adopted, only counted; Steps 288-291 remain unchanged (all R6).

b_rows_sample.anchor: SIX independent routes, six methods, one conclusion: no established order on \Sigma or K. ... third independent arrival
b_rows_sample.statement: The thought experiment, walking the model forward from the inside, independently hits two of the programme's known open results: (a) it re-states 'Sigma(K_{t+1}) succ Sigma(K_t), where the ordering still needs to be mathematically established' -- a sixth independent route (after Sigma-axis measurement per Step 291, executed retraction, Step 060 sec60.71, Step 274.32, and the Pareto refusal in artifact 21) to the conclusion there is no established order on Sigma or K; (b) it re-derives invariant I-V (Decision correctness != Outcome correctness, via the rollback example) -- a third independent arrival (after corpus inspection and the Vairagya R6 finding in Step 286), corpus-supported by 42.9/42.41, one of only two invariants testable today. Assessed as the strongest form of corroboration this track can produce: independent re-derivation of an already-CORPUS-SUPPORTED invariant, though the source did not realize I-V already existed.

b_rows_sample.anchor: All 22 registry operations change VALUES or MEMBERSHIP. NONE restructures the interpretive frame.
b_rows_sample.statement: Connects Reframe to artifact 21's K_t=(D_t,V_t,...) distinction between dimension discovery (D_t->D_{t+1}) and value improvement (v_t(d)->v_{t+1}(d)): Reframe is D_t->D_t' with V_t reinterpreted -- the same distinction seen from a different chapter. Observes all 22 registry operations change values or membership; none restructures the interpretive frame. Two independent sources (the purification file and Ch2) now say state change includes restructuring, and the registry has no operation of that kind -- registered as O-Q3, a gap in O's coverage distinct from its membership rule (N-4). Also notes Ch2's Knowledge!=Decision!=Action!=Result corroborates Ch18's five-way separation (artifact 25) and Step 256.21's Command!=Transformation, and that Ch2 opens by restating the ratified N notin K_t -- continuity with the ratified base, not a parallel ontology.

a_notations: Y_purify = Q o C o R o E o Z
b_aliases: fifth arrival at no total order on K

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'gita-pareto-order-dimension-value-audit' POSSIBLY relates to 'epistemic-purification-operator-algebra' (batch B0054). Note: Research artifact 21 audits S2226 (purification) and S2228 (sentence!=dimension) against the formal lane. Identifies S2226's refusal of v_{t+1}>v_t as a Pareto-dominance problem (K_{t+1} succeq_Pareto K_t iff no dimension worse and some strictly better -- a partial order admitting incomparability), the FIFTH independent route (of five) to the conclusion there is no total order on K, and merges the previously separate gaps M-Q3 (no metric) and M-Q4 (no loss function) into one decision M-Q3prime (heterogeneous dimensions with differing improvement directions admit no scalar without a normative weighting). Identifies that S2228's dimension/value distinction exposes an unstated presupposition inside the ratified result equiv_D (264.15): equiv_D silently presupposes a dimension object, which (unlike Proposition) is not among the ratified eight primitives -- registered as open question D-Q1. Flags K_t=(D_t,V_t,R_t,P_t,...) as an open-ended tuple violating 258.35's extensional-definition warning (D-Q2). Counts a sixth disjoint operation vocabulary {E,R,C,X,Q,Z} (G-91), noting Qualify appears in both this and the S2219/S2227 Omega_K algebra (G-92), reinforcing that any minimal kernel algebra containing Qualify inherits G1.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We now change mode. The previous steps established the target architecture. Step 109 begins the reconstruction of the actual KnowledgeOS/EKS system. The governing principle is: No architectural assertion without evidence.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the governing principle for Step 109's methodological shift from target-architecture definition to actual-system reconstruction: no architectural assertion without evidence.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We will therefore distinguish rigorously between Observed, Inferred, Specified, Claimed, and Not yet evidenced.
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces a five-way epistemic status distinction: Observed, Inferred, Specified, Claimed, Not-yet-evidenced.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.1 — The reconstruction question ... What software, artifacts, processes and runtime mechanisms actually constitute KnowledgeOS today? K_actual=Artifacts+Code+Configuration+Workflows+RuntimeBehavior. We then compare K_actual↔K_intended.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reframes the guiding question as K_actual=Artifacts+Code+Configuration+Workflows+RuntimeBehavior, compared against K_intended.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.2 — Evidence sources ... repository structure; configuration; source code; schemas/migrations; APIs; tests; CI/CD; agent harnesses; generated artifacts; runtime/operational evidence. No single category is sufficient.
a_rows_sample.statement: Lists ten evidence sources in increasing behavioral strength, stating no single category is sufficient alone.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.3 — Evidence classification ... E0 Name only, E1 Structural evidence, E2 Implementation evidence, E3 Verification evidence, E4 Runtime evidence, E5 Governance evidence. The strongest conformance claim normally requires several levels.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a six-level evidence classification E0 (name only) through E5 (governance evidence).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.4 — Experiment 1 ... We discover knowledge/ directory. Can we conclude 'KnowledgeOS has a knowledge domain'? No. Expected: E0/E1. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: discovering a bare knowledge/ directory yields only E0/E1 evidence, not a knowledge-domain conclusion; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.5 — Experiment 2 ... Inside the directory we find KnowledgeRepository, KnowledgeService, KnowledgeController. Expected: implementation evidence for a knowledge-related capability, but not yet proof it is the authoritative KnowledgeOS knowledge layer. Result: E2
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2: finding named knowledge-related classes gives E2 implementation evidence without proving authoritative status.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.6 — Experiment 3 ... Tests demonstrate KnowledgeServiceTest and CI executes them. Expected: E3. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: CI-executed tests yield E3 verification evidence; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.7 — Experiment 4 ... Production records demonstrate actual knowledge operations. Expected: E4. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 4: production records demonstrating actual operations yield E4 runtime evidence; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.8 — Experiment 5 ... Architecture governance explicitly identifies the component as authoritative. Expected: E5. Only now do we have a strong chain: Structure→Implementation→Verification→Runtime→Governance.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: explicit governance identification yields E5, completing the strong evidence chain Structure→Implementation→Verification→Runtime→Governance.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.9 — Actual component inventory ... ComponentInventory_actual. Each component gets Component ID, Name, Location, Type, Responsibility, Dependencies, Knowledge role, Governance role, Agent role, Runtime role, Evidence, Confidence, Status.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the ActualComponentInventory schema with 13 attributes per component (ID, Name, Location, Type, Responsibility, Dependencies, Knowledge/Governance/Agent/Runtime roles, Evidence, Confidence, Status).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.10 — Component classification ... Knowledge, Ingestion, Semantic processing, Governance, Agent integration, Assurance, Storage, Runtime infrastructure, Interface, Operational tooling.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines ten semantic component categories: Knowledge, Ingestion, Semantic processing, Governance, Agent integration, Assurance, Storage, Runtime infrastructure, Interface, Operational tooling.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.11 — Important rule ... A component can have more than one role. AgentGateway may be AgentIntegration+SecurityBoundary+API. We should not force artificial classification.
a_rows_sample.statement: States components can hold multiple roles simultaneously (e.g. AgentGateway = AgentIntegration+SecurityBoundary+API), forbidding forced single-category classification.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.12 — Repository topology ... What is the actual repository topology? We must derive the actual tree from evidence rather than assume this structure exists.
a_rows_sample.statement: States repository topology must be derived from evidence, not assumed.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.13 — Experiment 6 ... Documentation describes knowledge/governance/agents. Repository actually contains app/packages/scripts. Expected: the repository structure wins for the implementation topology. Result: PASS. Documentation remains evidence of intended architecture.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 6: when documented and actual repository structures diverge, actual structure wins for implementation topology while documentation remains evidence of intent; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.14 — Repository boundaries ... Is KnowledgeOS one repository? multiple repositories? a platform plus consumers? This cannot be assumed.
a_rows_sample.statement: States repository boundaries (single repo, multiple repos, platform-plus-consumers, etc.) cannot be assumed and must be established.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.15 — Experiment 7 ... Claude harness is in one repository. KnowledgeOS backend is in another. Expected: they may still constitute one logical ecosystem, but we must distinguish RepositoryBoundary from SystemBoundary. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 7: separately-repository'd Claude harness and KnowledgeOS backend may still form one logical ecosystem, distinguishing RepositoryBoundary from SystemBoundary; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.16 — System boundary ... KnowledgeOS_SystemBoundary containing all components demonstrably part of the ecosystem: EKS+KnowledgeOS+AgentHarnesses+Governance+Assurance. But each inclusion must be evidenced.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines KnowledgeOS_SystemBoundary as the evidenced union of demonstrably-related components (potentially EKS+KnowledgeOS+AgentHarnesses+Governance+Assurance), each inclusion requiring evidence.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.17 — Experiment 8 ... A generic CI tool is used by KnowledgeOS. Does that make the CI tool a KnowledgeOS component? No. Expected: External dependency unless the architecture explicitly treats it as internal. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8: a generic CI tool used by KnowledgeOS remains an external dependency unless explicitly treated as internal; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 109.18 — Dependency versus component ... Uses(X,Y) does not imply Y∈KnowledgeOS. We need to distinguish InternalComponent from ExternalDependency.
a_rows_sample.statement: States Uses(X,Y) does not imply membership Y∈KnowledgeOS, distinguishing InternalComponent from ExternalDependency.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Status(I) in {Implemented, Partial, Specified, Missing, Unknown} ... Unknown != Missing ... Unknown != Implemented
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a five-value implementation-status classification for every architectural property (Implemented/Partial/Specified/Missing/Unknown), with boxed guardrails Unknown!=Missing and Unknown!=Implemented -- the distinction between Missing and Unknown is called critical.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We derive a good architectural principle and gradually begin speaking about it as though the existing system already implements it. That would be architectural hallucination ... Derived Architecture != Current Architecture
b_rows_sample.statement: Names the risk of 'architectural hallucination' -- gradually treating a derived architectural principle as though the existing system already implements it -- and sets a strict boundary Derived Architecture != Current Architecture, requiring the current architecture to be established from evidence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: G_i=(I_i,Status,Owner,Mechanism,Evidence,Confidence,Gap)
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a per-invariant evidence record G_i=(Invariant,Status,Owner,Mechanism,Evidence,Confidence,Gap) as the unit of the architecture audit.

b_rows_sample.anchor: I1 Identity ≠ State ... I15 No silent semantic strengthening ... none of these should yet be marked 'Implemented' merely because we derived them
b_rows_sample.statement: Lists a first 15-item theoretical assurance register (I1-I15: Identity!=State, historical version preservation, provenance preservation, epistemic status preservation, Unknown!=False, uncertainty preservation, model-version integrity, Inference!=Authority, Decision!=Execution, Execution!=Outcome, contradiction preservation, temporal validity, legal state transitions, pre/postconditions, no silent semantic strengthening), explicitly marked as targets not yet verified as implemented.

b_rows_sample.anchor: E_0=No evidence ... E_5=Formal verification
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a six-level evidence-quality hierarchy E0 (no evidence) through E5 (formal verification), via E1 claim/documentation, E2 static implementation evidence, E3 executable test evidence, E4 runtime/production evidence, worked through a provenance example progressing from documentation claim to automated evidence-chain test to production lineage recording.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Confidence(I) != EvidenceLevel(I)
b_rows_sample.statement: Separates evidence strength from confidence: strong (E2) evidence from inspecting only one module may still leave confidence in system-wide enforcement low; Confidence(I) != EvidenceLevel(I).

b_rows_sample.anchor: The architecture is 82% compliant ... unless we have first defined ... population ... weighting ... independence ... evidence quality ... confidence model ... treatment of critical properties
b_rows_sample.statement: Warns against stating an unsupported compliance percentage (e.g. '82% compliant') without first defining the requirement population, weighting, independence, evidence quality, confidence model and treatment of critical properties; recommends a qualitative CriticalGap measure instead.

b_rows_sample.anchor: G1 — Semantic gap ... G5 — Assurance gap ... These gaps can coexist
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes five coexisting gap classes: G1 Semantic (software loses domain meaning), G2 Governance (authority/responsibility ambiguous), G3 Temporal (historical state not reconstructable), G4 Epistemic (evidence/uncertainty/assumptions lost), G5 Assurance (behavior may be correct but insufficiently evidenced).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Implementation = Present but Assurance = Weak. This is not necessarily an implementation gap. It is an: Assurance Gap
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example distinguishing implementation presence from assurance: modelVersion correctly stored (Implementation=Present) but with no automated test proving it survives the workflow (Assurance=Weak) is classified specifically as an Assurance Gap, not an implementation gap.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ArchitectureGap != ImplementationGap != VerificationGap
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Architecture gap (design itself lacks the mechanism), Implementation gap (mechanism specified but code does not implement it correctly), and Verification gap (implementation appears correct but evidence is insufficient) as three non-identical gap types.

b_rows_sample.anchor: TechnicalCapability=Present while GovernanceCapability=Missing ... Ownerless Invariants ... Shared responsibility must not mean undefined responsibility
b_rows_sample.statement: Identifies a governance gap pattern where a technical mechanism (AI->Assessment->Approval) works but nobody has defined who is authorized to approve, so TechnicalCapability=Present while GovernanceCapability=Missing; introduces the 'ownerless invariant' search (Owner(I)=empty set, dangerous because nobody maintains it) and its converse, the 'shared ownership' problem, where undivided shared responsibility (Owner(I)={A,B,C}) risks each team assuming another enforces the invariant -- boxed as 'shared responsibility must not mean undefined responsibility'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: L(C)=InformationBefore(C)-InformationAfter(C) ... Loss(C)={p | p in CriticalProperties and p absent after transformation}
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a semantic-loss function for a context-to-context contract L(C)=InformationBefore(C)-InformationAfter(C), refined to Loss(C) as the set of critical properties absent after transformation; worked example: an Assessment=(score,uncertainty,modelVersion,evidenceRef) contract sending only {score} loses uncertainty/modelVersion/evidenceRef, a Critical Semantic Gap if downstream governance requires them.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ΔT=T_target △ T_actual where △ denotes symmetric difference ... Unauthorized State Transition Path
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes reconstructing actual state-machine transitions T_actual from implementation and comparing to target transitions T_target via symmetric difference DeltaT = T_target triangle T_actual as a state-transition gap measure; a transition present in T_actual but absent from T_target is an Unauthorized State Transition Path warranting high priority when governance consequences exist.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Replay(A,t)=F(Data_t,Policy_t,Model_t,Schema_t,Context_t) ... Reproducibility ... Replayability ... A system may be replayable without being perfectly reproducible
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines historical replay Replay(A,t)=F(Data_t,Policy_t,Model_t,Schema_t,Context_t), noting exact replay (Replay(A,t)=A_t) may be impossible when external conditions change, in which case the system should preserve enough provenance to explain why; distinguishes Reproducibility (can we regenerate the same result, F(X,M)=Y again) from Replayability (can we reconstruct what happened and why), noting a system may be replayable without being reproducible (e.g. a now-defunct external service).

b_rows_sample.anchor: A new state does not necessarily know the old state ... CurrentState + HistoricalProvenance ... History must be preservable, not necessarily embedded in every current state
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives a technically disciplined reading of an earlier 'Chapter 4' observation ('a new state does not necessarily know the old state'): rejects CurrentState=History, proposing instead CurrentState+HistoricalProvenance as sufficient for reconstructing relevant prior meaning; boxed principle: history must be preservable, not necessarily embedded in every current state.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Prediction -> AutomaticAuthority ... CurrentState -> AssumeCompleteHistory ... Unknown -> False ... Execution -> AssumeSuccess ... Architecture=AllowedTransitions+ForbiddenTransitions
b_rows_sample.statement: States a negative-space design principle: a mature architecture must specify ForbiddenPaths as well as AllowedPaths (Architecture=AllowedTransitions+ForbiddenTransitions), and lists four named forbidden implicit transitions to guard against: Prediction->AutomaticAuthority, CurrentState->AssumeCompleteHistory, Unknown->False, Execution->AssumeSuccess.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Assessment -/-> Authority ... The X is important. It represents a path that the architecture must prevent
b_rows_sample.statement: Extends the Step 211 Architecture Assurance Graph with an explicit forbidden-path marker: Evidence->Assessment->Governance->Decision->Authorized Action->Execution->Outcome, with an explicit forbidden edge Assessment-/->Authority that the architecture must prevent.

b_rows_sample.anchor: G-01 Identity ... G-15 History ... This is the audit instrument
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a 15-item provisional gap register (G-01 through G-15) as concrete audit questions (identity/state separation, historical reconstructability, provenance traceability, uncertainty preservation across boundaries, model/version provenance, inference-to-authority escalation, decision/execution separation, execution/outcome separation, illegal transition blocking, contract semantic loss, contradiction coexistence, unknown-vs-false distinguishability, automatic critical-invariant testing, single accountable ownership, prior semantic context reconstruction).

b_rows_sample.anchor: No evidence => Unknown. Not: No evidence => Missing. And certainly not: No evidence => Implemented
b_rows_sample.statement: States the methodological rule of Step 212 as most important: the gap register's rows must not be populated by imagination but from actual KnowledgeOS artifacts, with the default for absence of evidence being No evidence=>Unknown, explicitly not =>Missing and certainly not =>Implemented.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ### Architectural reasoning PASS ... Gītā Chapters 1–4 COHERENT
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 212 verdict: architectural reasoning, DDD, mathematics, statistics, and AI dimensions each rated PASS; Gita chapters 1-4 rated COHERENT (continuing to generate architectural questions without being presented as technical proof).

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels share the notation 'E0..E5'

a_rows_sample.anchor: We now cross the important boundary: Conceptual model \rightarrow Executable state machine. The purpose of 25A.4 is not to build production KnowledgeOS. It is to see whether our current mathematical model can actually execute a sequence of knowledge transitions without violating the invariants disco
a_rows_sample.statement: Announces crossing from conceptual model to executable state machine, testing whether a sequence of knowledge transitions can execute without violating prior invariants.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The experiment ... K_0 \xrightarrow{event_1} K_1 \xrightarrow{event_2} K_2 \cdots \xrightarrow{event_n} K_n. Every transition must be explicit; reproducible; traceable; temporally identifiable; reversible/replayable through history; unable to silently change historical states. The fundamental functi
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the fundamental transition function T(K_t,e_t)→K_{t+1} required to be explicit, reproducible, traceable, temporally identifiable, replayable, and unable to silently mutate history.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Minimal state ... K_t = (A_t,E_t,Q_t,C_t,D_t,V_t) ... Assertions, Evidence, Assessments, Conflicts, Derivation/dependency relations, Temporal validity. And outside K_t: G for the current goal, and EC for the epistemic contract. This is intentionally small.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the minimal six-field executable KnowledgeState K_t=(Assertions,Evidence,Assessments,Conflicts,Derivations,TemporalValidity) with Goal and EpistemicContract kept external.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Immutable snapshots ... K0 = empty, K1 = K0 + Evidence E1 + Assertion A1, K2 = K1 + Evidence E2 + Assertion A2, K3 = K2 + Conflict C1, K4 = K3 + Resolution R1, K5 = K4 + Retraction E1. We never execute K1.modify(...). Instead K1 → K2.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a worked six-snapshot immutable state sequence (K0-K5), explicitly forbidding in-place mutation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Event model ... EvidenceRegistered, AssertionCreated, AssessmentRecorded, AssertionCommitted, ConflictDetected, ConflictResolved, EvidenceInvalidated, AssertionSuperseded, AssertionRetracted, DerivationCreated, SnapshotCreated. This is already revealing something important: KnowledgeState is natural
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines an eleven-event vocabulary, observing that KnowledgeState is naturally event-evolvable (mathematically compatible with event sourcing) without committing to it as a production implementation choice.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 1 — Empty state ... K_0=\varnothing. We calculate Hash(K_0)=h_0. The hash is not the mathematical state itself. It gives us a useful integrity mechanism for the experiment. ... Experiment 2 — Register evidence ... e_1=EvidenceRegistered(E_1). T(K_0,e_1)=K_1. E_1\in K_1. But A_1\notin K_1
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 1 (empty state with an integrity hash) and Experiment 2 (evidence registration), confirming evidence entering K1 does not automatically create the corresponding assertion — registering evidence does not automatically create knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 3 — Assessment ... q_1=Assess(E_1,A_1). relevance = high, directness = direct, temporal_fit = valid, authenticity = verified, dependency = independent, conflict = none. Then Q_1(A_1)=q_1. Still A_1 is not necessarily committed. ... Experiment 4 — Commitment ... e_3=Commit(A_1). Subject to
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 3 (assessment with six concrete field values) and Experiment 4 (contract-gated commitment producing an explicit commitment boundary K3∋A1).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 5 — Duplicate evidence ... E_1'=E_1. We require Register(E_1')=NoSemanticDuplicate. Register(Register(E))=Register(E) at least with respect to semantic state. This is an idempotency requirement.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 5 testing idempotent duplicate registration: Register(Register(E))=Register(E) with respect to semantic state.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 6 — Independent corroboration ... E_2 from an independent direct observation. E_1\vdash A_1 and E_2\vdash A_1. The system should increase the evidential support for A_1, but must not simply count sources. We need Independence(E_1,E_2). This confirms the earlier statistical requirement.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 6 (independent corroboration) confirming that increasing evidential support requires an explicit Independence(E1,E2) check, not simple source counting.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 7 — Contradiction ... E_3: Version(Nexus)=3.72.0. Create A_2. Now A_1\perp A_2 under the same context/time. Generate C_1=Conflict(A_1,A_2). The state becomes K_4=\{A_1,A_2,C_1\}. Both remain visible.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 7 (contradiction) producing K4={A1,A2,C1} with both assertions and the conflict marker retained.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 8 — Temporal resolution ... A_1: Version=3.69 [t_0,t_1] ... A_2: Version=3.72 [t_2,\infty) where t_1<t_2. Re-evaluate Conflict(A_1,A_2). Result: False. This is an extremely important result. The conflict engine must operate on semantic scope, not simply values.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 8 showing disjoint validity intervals resolve the apparent conflict to False, called an extremely important result: the conflict engine must operate on semantic scope, not raw values.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 9 — Evidence invalidation ... the inventory from which it came is discovered to have been faulty. e_9=Invalidate(E_1). K_5=T(K_4,e_9). But we do not delete E_1. Instead E1.status = Invalid and Dependents(E_1) are identified. ... Dependency propagation ... E_1\rightarrow A_1\rightarrow A_4
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 9 (invalidation without deletion, E1.status=Invalid) followed by dependency propagation producing an Impact(E1) reassessment cascade through the derivation chain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 10 — Partial support survives ... Support(A_1)=\{E_1,E_2\}. Invalidate E_1. Then Support(A_1)=\{E_2\}. If E_2 is sufficient: Status(A_1)=Supported. If not: Status(A_1)=Uncertain. Retraction(E)\not\Rightarrow Retraction(A) automatically. This is a major invariant.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 10 showing partial support survival after one evidence item is invalidated, establishing the major invariant Retraction(E) ⇏ Retraction(A) automatically.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 11 — Derived assertion ... A_1 and A_5. Rule: A_1\land A_5\Rightarrow A_6. Record D_1=(A_1,A_5\vdash A_6). Now invalidate A_1. We must automatically identify A_6 as affected.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 11 (derived assertion) requiring automatic identification of a downstream derived assertion (A6) as affected when a premise (A1) is invalidated.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 12 — Knowledge can become unknown ... A_1.status=Committed. After invalidation of its only support: A_1.status=Unknown. Not False. Not Deleted. Known \rightarrow Unknown is a valid knowledge transition.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 12 (one of the most important tests) establishing Known→Unknown as a valid knowledge transition, distinct from becoming False or Deleted.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 13 — Historical state ... K_3 contained A_1. Later K_6 does not accept A_1. We must still be able to query K_3\models A_1. HistoricalState(K_3) remains unchanged. This passes our historical immutability requirement.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 13 confirming a superseded historical snapshot remains queryable and unchanged, passing the historical immutability requirement.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 14 — Replay ... Replay(K_0,e_1,\ldots,e_6)=K_6. This gives us Replayability. If replay produces a different state K_6'\neq K_6, we have discovered a serious defect. ... Experiment 15 — Determinism ... T(K,e)=T(K,e) on repeated execution. Register(E_1) should produce the same semantic stat
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 14 (full replay reconstruction, framed as revealing a serious defect if the replayed state diverges) and Experiment 15 (determinism, T(K,e) reproducible on repeated execution).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 16 — AI output ... L_1="Rollback has been successfully verified." with no supporting artifact. Support(A_{AI})=\varnothing. Therefore Commit(A_{AI})=False. The assertion remains Candidate/Unsupported. The state machine survives the hallucination.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 16 confirming the state machine correctly rejects commitment of an unsupported LLM hallucination, remaining Candidate/Unsupported.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 17 — AI extraction ... Rollback test executed at 14:30. Restore completed successfully. AI extracts A_{AI2}: RollbackVerified=True. But provenance becomes A_{AI2} \rightarrow LLMExtraction \rightarrow Artifact \rightarrow Source. The LLM is recorded as a transformation, not as the ultimat
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 17 (legitimate LLM extraction from a real report) confirming the correct provenance chain A→LLMExtraction→Artifact→Source is achieved — exactly the intended architecture.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Experiment 18 — Historical decision ... K_{10} had Rollback=Unknown. A decision is made D_{10}=DoNotMigrate. At t_{11}, we learn Rollback=True. We must not alter D_{10}. Instead D_{10} remains the decision made under K_{10}. This passes the anti-hindsight invariant.
a_rows_sample.statement: Works Experiment 18 confirming the anti-hindsight invariant passes: a historical decision remains unaltered even after later evidence would have changed it.

b_rows_sample.anchor: An Observation is a recorded representation of something perceived, measured, detected, or otherwise encountered without automatically asserting its interpretation. O = (subject, method, value, time, context). Observation ≠ Interpretation. ... An observation must not silently contain an unmarked conclusion. ... An LLM frequently transforms: 'I found X' into: 'Therefore Y.' KnowledgeOS should preserve that boundary.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Observation = (subject, method, value, time, context) as a recorded representation without automatic interpretation, distinguished from Interpretation and further from Claim (three epistemic levels illustrated by 'Nexus process is listening on port 8081' vs 'Nexus is reachable by application clients' vs 'Nexus architecture permits direct application access'). States the invariant that an observation must not silently contain an unmarked conclusion, warning this is especially important for AI-generated material, which frequently collapses 'I found X' into 'Therefore Y.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: An Inquiry is an intentional epistemic activity directed toward answering a question or resolving uncertainty. I = (question, subject, scope, context, objective). ... Task ≠ Inquiry ... although an Inquiry can generate Tasks. ... Inquiry ⇒ Question/Object. A generic 'Analyze this.' is insufficiently specified unless the intended question can be recovered.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Inquiry = (question, subject, scope, context, objective) as an intentional epistemic activity ('determine something'), distinct from a Task ('do something'), though an Inquiry can generate Tasks (Task != Inquiry). Invariant: Inquiry implies Question/Object -- a generic instruction like 'Analyze this' is insufficiently specified unless its intended question can be recovered.

b_rows_sample.anchor: An observation becomes Evidence relative to an inquiry or claim. Evidence is contextual. E = (O, I, relevance, provenance, integrity). ... Evidence must preserve enough provenance to answer: Where did this come from? At minimum: Source(E) and Method(E). ... Evidence ≠ Proof unless the domain and method justify that terminology. We should use proof sparingly in the book.
b_rows_sample.statement: Evidence E = (Observation, Inquiry, relevance, provenance, integrity) is contextual -- an observation becomes evidence only relative to a specific inquiry/claim, and the same observation can be evidence for multiple inquiries. Minimum required provenance fields: Source(E), Method(E) (and for technical evidence, Time(E), Subject(E)). Distinguishes Evidence from mathematical Proof (Proof => Theorem under a formal system): engineering evidence is generally not equivalent to proof, and 'proof' should be used sparingly.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A governed representation of a claim or proposition whose source, context, validity and epistemic status are sufficiently known for the intended use. K = (claim, source, context, validity, status). ... Evidence supports Knowledge. but: Evidence ≢ Knowledge. ... Knowledge may have states such as: PROPOSED SUPPORTED CONFIRMED CONTESTED SUPERSEDED EXPIRED UNKNOWN ... K1 -- superseded by --> K2. Current truth ≠ Historical truth.
b_rows_sample.statement: Knowledge K = (claim, source, context, validity, status) is 'a governed representation of a claim or proposition whose source, context, validity and epistemic status are sufficiently known for the intended use'; Evidence supports Knowledge but Evidence is not identical to Knowledge. Candidate (non-final) knowledge-status enumeration: PROPOSED, SUPPORTED, CONFIRMED, CONTESTED, SUPERSEDED, EXPIRED, UNKNOWN. Superseded knowledge (K1 superseded-by K2) must not be erased, giving Current truth != Historical truth.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A Determination is a conclusion reached from specified knowledge/evidence under a defined context and method. D = f(K,E,C,M) ... A determination must be explainable. ... 'The AI said so' is not sufficient as a durable determination. ... VerificationResult → supports → Determination. But: VerificationResult ≠ Determination.
b_rows_sample.statement: Determination D=f(K,E,C,M) (knowledge, evidence, context, method) is a conclusion stronger than a casual opinion; invariant that a determination must be explainable via Determination -> Inputs+Method+Context, so 'the AI said so' cannot serve as a durable determination -- the system must be able to answer 'why did we reach this conclusion?' A deterministic VerificationResult (e.g. PASS) supports a Determination but is not identical to it (VerificationResult != Determination); a human/agent determination such as 'the implementation conforms to rule R' is a separate epistemic act built on top of the verification result.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A Decision is an authoritative selection among alternatives, made by an authorized decision-maker or mechanism within a defined governance context. Decision = (choice, authority, scope, context, time). ... Determination ≠ Decision ... Decision ⇒ Authority. ... Recommendation ≠ Decision. An AI may say: 'I recommend rejecting the architecture change.' That is a recommendation. It does not become an authoritative decision merely because the system generated it.
b_rows_sample.statement: Decision = (choice, authority, scope, context, time), an authoritative selection among alternatives made by an authorized decision-maker/mechanism within a governance context; a determination may inform but does not automatically become a decision (Determination != Decision); a decision requires identifiable authority (Decision => Authority, 'who or what had the right to decide?'); an AI recommendation is explicitly not a decision merely because the system generated it (Recommendation != Decision).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Authorization answers: Is this actor permitted to perform this operation under these conditions? Auth = f(actor, action, resource, policy, context, time). ... Decision ≠ Authorization. A governance body can decide that something should happen while an execution system separately authorizes a particular actor to perform it. ... Execute(a) ⇒ ValidAuthorization(a) unless an explicitly defined exception applies. ... Action ≠ Execution ... Execution(Action) produces observable effects.
b_rows_sample.statement: Authorization Auth=f(actor,action,resource,policy,context,time) answers whether a specific actor may perform a specific operation under specific conditions; Decision != Authorization (a governance decision that something should happen is separate from an execution system authorizing a particular actor). Invariant: Execute(a) => ValidAuthorization(a) unless an explicit exception applies. Action ('upgrade Nexus') != Execution ('podman pull ...', the mechanism); Execution(Action) produces observable effects, and Action->Execution->Observation closes the loop.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We started with nouns: Knowledge Evidence Decision Action and initially they looked like possible domain objects. But through the semantic analysis, we discovered that the more fundamental architecture is actually defined by relationships and invariants: supports derivedFrom determines authorizes executes supersedes contradicts observes. ... The domain is not merely: Objects. It is: Objects + Relationships + Invariants + Time + Authority.
b_rows_sample.statement: Major DDD observation: what began as candidate domain-object nouns (Knowledge, Evidence, Decision, Action) turned out, under semantic analysis, to be more fundamentally characterized by named relationships (supports, derivedFrom, determines, authorizes, executes, supersedes, contradicts, observes) and invariants; the domain is therefore relation-centric -- Objects + Relationships + Invariants + Time + Authority -- rather than a plain object model, judged 'much closer to the actual problem KnowledgeOS is trying to solve.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: I1: Observation ≠ Interpretation I2: Evidence ≠ Knowledge I3: Determination ≠ Decision I4: Decision ≠ Authorization I5: Authorization ≠ Execution I6: Unknown ≠ False I7: Provenance ≠ Lineage I8: Memory ≠ Historical Continuity I9: Recommendation ≠ Decision I10: Evidence must be traceable to its source. These should become candidates for the KnowledgeOS semantic constitution.
b_rows_sample.statement: Consolidates a candidate ten-invariant set (I1-I10: Observation!=Interpretation, Evidence!=Knowledge, Determination!=Decision, Decision!=Authorization, Authorization!=Execution, Unknown!=False, Provenance!=Lineage, Memory!=Historical Continuity, Recommendation!=Decision, Evidence must be traceable to its source), explicitly proposed as candidates for a future 'KnowledgeOS semantic constitution' -- not yet ratified.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We have not yet decided: exact bounded contexts; exact aggregates; database schema; event model; API structure; graph technology; microservices; class hierarchy; whether Wisdom deserves its own model; exact implementation of epistemic states. Those decisions belong later. ... Which invariants require a bounded context, which require an aggregate, which require a policy, and which are merely semantic relationships? ... Semantic Contract → Invariant → Consistency Boundary → DDD Boundary.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 161 explicitly restrains scope: it has not decided exact bounded contexts, aggregates, database schema, event model, API structure, graph technology, microservices, class hierarchy, whether Wisdom deserves its own model, or the exact implementation of epistemic states -- deferred to later steps. Proposes Step 162 (Invariant and Boundary Derivation) to ask, per invariant, whether it requires a bounded context, an aggregate, a policy, or is merely a semantic relationship, via the pipeline Semantic Contract -> Invariant -> Consistency Boundary -> DDD Boundary.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 1. Recover/save the DeepSeek outputs. 2. Preserve them as external research evidence. 3. Classify each proposed connection. 4. Separate: already established.../compatible external interpretation/potentially useful hypothesis/unsupported speculation/contradiction. 5. Independently verify anything we want to incorporate. 6. In particular, the idea: "Zero is a boundary operator" must not quietly become KnowledgeOS architecture merely because DeepSeek proposed it.
a_rows_sample.statement: Specifies a seven-step DeepSeek-research intake process kept deliberately outside the current book-production stream: recover/save outputs, preserve as external research evidence, classify each proposed connection, sort into five categories (already established by KnowledgeOS evidence / compatible external interpretation / potentially useful hypothesis / unsupported speculation / contradiction), independently verify anything considered for incorporation, create a formal intake/research gate, and only then decide inclusion in Edition 2; gives the named example "Zero is a boundary operator" as an idea that must not quietly become architecture merely because DeepSeek proposed it, though it may become a research hypothesis if it survives the process.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS should not begin with: Choose mathematics -> Build architecture. The correct direction: Observe knowledge behavior -> Discover invariants -> Find mathematical structures that describe them
b_rows_sample.statement: Mathematics should describe, not define: invariants must be discovered from observed knowledge behavior first, and mathematical structures found afterward to describe them -- never the reverse order.

b_rows_sample.statement: Document-wide status discipline: everything in this conceptual foundation document is Candidate/Hypothesis input to a future P4 Constitutional Invariant Map; nothing is adopted or SHALL; the existing EKS baseline (the 'f0106657' precedent) is untouched.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We now cross the most important bridge so far ... M_A→M_F→A→I. I ⊨ M_F meaning that the implementation satisfies the formal specification.
a_rows_sample.statement: Frames Step 91's central bridge M_A (abstract model)→M_F (formal specification)→A (architecture)→I (implementation), with the goal I ⊨ M_F.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.1 — Abstraction ... R=(id,type,actor,evidence,status). We need an abstraction function alpha:I→M. What mathematical object does this software state represent?
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines an abstraction function α:I→M mapping implementation state (e.g. a database GovernanceRequest entity) to its mathematical model meaning.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.2 — Experiment 1 ... Two database records differ internally (created_at). Mathematical model ignores creation time. Expected: alpha(A)=alpha(B). Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: two implementation records differing only in an irrelevant field (created_at) map to the same abstract state α(A)=α(B); result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.3 — Representation invariant ... RI(I). Approved ⇒ ValidApprovalExists.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the representation invariant RI(I), e.g. Approved ⇒ ValidApprovalExists, constraining which implementation states are valid.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.4 — Experiment 2 ... status=Approved but approval_id=NULL. Expected: RI(I)=False. Result: PASS. This is an invalid implementation state.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2: status=Approved with approval_id=NULL violates RI(I)=False, an invalid implementation state; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.5 — Refinement ... Behaviors(C) ⊆ Refinement(Behaviors(A)). The implementation may contain additional technical detail, but it must not introduce forbidden semantic behavior.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines refinement: a concrete implementation C refines abstract specification A if Behaviors(C) ⊆ Refinement(Behaviors(A)) — extra technical detail allowed, forbidden semantic behavior not.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.6 — Experiment 3 ... Abstract spec: Unapproved ↛ Production. Implementation introduces forceDeploy() allowing Unapproved→Production. Expected: RefinementFailure. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: a forceDeploy() function allowing Unapproved→Production, forbidden by the abstract specification, is RefinementFailure; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.7 — This is the critical bridge ... Software architecture is not merely an implementation choice. It is a refinement of the mathematical/institutional model.
a_rows_sample.statement: States software architecture is not merely an implementation choice but a refinement of the mathematical/institutional model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.8 — Preconditions ... Pre(x). Pre(Approve(r))=Submitted(r) ∧ AuthorizedActor(actor).
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines preconditions Pre(x), e.g. Pre(Approve(r))=Submitted(r) ∧ AuthorizedActor(actor).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.9 — Experiment 4 ... Approve(r) requires Submitted(r)=True. Input Draft(r). Expected: Approve(r) must not execute as a valid transition. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 4: calling Approve(r) on a Draft(r) (violating the Submitted precondition) must not be a valid transition; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.10 — Postconditions ... Post(x,f(x)). Post: Approved(r) ∧ AuthorizedDecisionExists(r).
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines postconditions Post(x,f(x)), e.g. Post: Approved(r) ∧ AuthorizedDecisionExists(r).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.11 — Experiment 5 ... Approval function returns successfully. But no approval record exists. Expected: Post=False. Result: PASS. The implementation is incorrect even though the method technically returned success.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: an approval function returning success without creating an approval record violates Post=False; the implementation is incorrect despite a technically-successful return; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.12 — Hoare logic ... {P} C {Q}. If precondition P holds, execution of command C establishes postcondition Q. {Submitted(r)∧Authorized(a)} Approve(r,a) {Approved(r)∧AuthorizedApprovalExists(r)}.
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces Hoare triples {P} C {Q} to express governance operation contracts, e.g. {Submitted∧Authorized} Approve(r,a) {Approved∧AuthorizedApprovalExists}.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.13 — Experiment 6 ... Implementation satisfies the method signature but violates the postcondition. Expected: FormalContractViolation. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 6: satisfying a method signature while violating its postcondition is FormalContractViolation; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.14 — Invariants ... Approved ⇒ Reviewed. I(s)=True forall s in ReachableStates.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a state invariant (e.g. Approved ⇒ Reviewed) that must hold I(s)=True for all reachable states s.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.15 — Experiment 7 ... System begins in a valid state. After 100 transitions, one state contains Approved without Reviewed. Expected: InvariantViolation. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 7: after 100 transitions, a reached state with Approved but not Reviewed violates the invariant; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.16 — Reachability matters ... forall s in Reachable(S_0): I(s). This is where the model-checking work from Step 89 becomes directly useful.
a_rows_sample.statement: States invariant checking requires forall s in Reachable(S_0): I(s), not just checking the initial state, explicitly linking to Step 89's model checking.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.17 — Experiment 8 ... Initial state satisfies every invariant. A sequence of valid-looking operations reaches an invalid state. Expected: the invariant is not actually preserved. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8: a valid-looking operation sequence reaching an invariant-violating state shows the invariant is not actually preserved; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.18 — State-transition refinement ... Submitted --Approve--> Approved. Implementation has many operations (loadRequest, validate, checkAuthority, createApproval, updateStatus, emitEvent, invalidateCache) but collectively they must refine Submitted→Approved.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines state-transition refinement: a multi-step implementation (loadRequest, validate, checkAuthority, createApproval, updateStatus, emitEvent, invalidateCache) must collectively refine the abstract transition Submitted→Approved.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 91.19 — Experiment 9 ... Implementation performs all technical operations correctly. But it changes Submitted→Rejected. Expected: it does not refine the intended abstract transition. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 9: technically-correct operations that end up transitioning Submitted→Rejected instead of →Approved fail to refine the intended transition; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Property-based/state-machine/negative/atomicity/replay/idempotency/temporal testing methodology
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes testing universally quantified properties (for-all x in Domain: P(x)) rather than only example->expected pairs -- e.g. for-all C: Validated(C) ⇒ Provenance(C)!=empty, checked over many generated claims. Randomly generates valid command sequences C1,...,Cn and requires I(X_i)=True after every transition, treating any invariant failure as a discovered counterexample -- 'substantially stronger than manual testing'. Adds negative property testing (generate invalid commands, e.g. Execute(ProposedDecision), expect Rejected, and require the machine not partially mutate state while erroring); an atomicity property (a failed command leaves X_before=X_after, i.e. FailedTransition ⇒ NoPartialDomainMutation); a replay property (Replay(H)=X_n for deterministic reconstruction) while ReplayState != ReplaySideEffects; an idempotency test (executing the same command twice yields X2=X1 w.r.t. the protected side effect); a temporal test (decision basis remains K_t1 despite a later knowledge update at t2); a contradiction test (E1|=C, E2|=not-C represented as Conflict(C), never arbitrarily resolved); and an uncertainty test (P(C)=0.6 must not become C=True absent an explicit domain threshold rule).

b_rows_sample.anchor: AI test: AIProposal cannot Execute directly but succeeds through Validation/Decision/Authorization; epistemic firewall stated as a measurable property
b_rows_sample.statement: Specifies the AI test: AIProposal -> Execute directly is expected Rejected, while AIProposal -> Validation -> Decision -> Authorization -> Execute is expected Accepted -- 'the AI is now inside the experiment, but not part of the mathematical authority', letting AI failure be tested without destroying domain integrity. Specifies the AI-hallucination experiment: a deliberately unsupported claim C_H with absent/invalid provenance must have Status(C_H) != Validated and therefore cannot drive an authorized action -- giving the epistemic firewall an experimentally measurable form: untrusted generation cannot cross into authoritative state without satisfying domain transitions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 91.30 — Property-based testing ... Instead of testing only examples, we define a property P(x). Then generate many valid and invalid instances.
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces property-based testing: defining a property P(x) and generating many valid/invalid instances rather than testing only fixed examples.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 91.31 — Experiment 14 ... Generate 10,000 random governance states. Check Approved⇒ValidApproval. Expected: any counterexample reveals a potential implementation defect. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 14: property-based testing over 10,000 random governance states checking Approved⇒ValidApproval; any counterexample reveals a potential defect; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 91.32 — Property testing is not proof ... Finding no counterexample among 10,000 tests does not establish forall x:P(x). It provides empirical evidence.
b_rows_sample.statement: States property-based testing provides only empirical evidence, not proof: passing 10,000 tests does not establish ∀x:P(x).

b_rows_sample.anchor: 91.33 — Experiment 15 ... 100,000 tests pass. System claims FormalProof=True. Expected: incorrect. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 15: claiming FormalProof=True after 100,000 passing tests is incorrect; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 91.34 — Test evidence has its own epistemic status ... TestResult with Coverage, Generator, Environment, Version, Timestamp. This fits naturally into KnowledgeOS provenance.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines TestResult as carrying its own provenance (Coverage, Generator, Environment, Version, Timestamp), fitting the broader KnowledgeOS provenance model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 91.35 — Model-based testing ... mathematical state machine M. Generate test sequences tau_1..tau_n from M. Execute against implementation I. Compare Behavior(I,tau) with Behavior(M,tau).
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines model-based testing: generating test sequences from state machine M and comparing Behavior(I,τ) against Behavior(M,τ).

b_rows_sample.anchor: 91.36 — Experiment 16 ... Model: Approved→Implemented. Implementation instead permits Approved→Cancelled without authorization. Expected: model-based test detects divergence. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 16: model-based testing detects an implementation divergence (unauthorized Approved→Cancelled instead of Approved→Implemented); result PASS.
