a_rows_sample.anchor: N_viol(R)=0 <=> H_hat(Q|R)=0, not merely N_viol=0 => H_hat(Q|R)=0 ... The asymmetry is diagnostic rather than logical.
a_rows_sample.statement: Strengthens a stated implication into a full equivalence: for finite empirical support, N_viol(R)=0 and H_hat(Q|R)=0 are logically equivalent adequacy conditions (since zero conditional entropy forces every observed R-fiber to a single Q-value and vice versa), but the two remain diagnostically distinct -- N_viol as a structural witness locating collisions, H_hat(Q|R) as an information summary of remaining uncertainty.

a_rows_sample.anchor: R_{n*} is adequate, R_{n*-1} is inadequate, B_{n*}: R_{n*} -> R_{n*-1}. If adequacy is non-monotone across the chain, record that as an experimental finding rather than assuming a single boundary.
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires the boundary transition B_{n*} to be defined only when both the adjacency condition (R_{n*} adequate) and its failure (R_{n*-1} inadequate) are established, distinguishing 'lowest adequate level,' 'first preservation failure,' and 'boundary transition' as three concepts that coincide only under monotone preservation behaviour across the reduction chain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: H(R|Q)>0 => R contains variation not determined by Q ... This variation is Q-extraneous relative to the inquiry, but is not necessarily useless information.
a_rows_sample.statement: Refines the interpretation of H(R|Q)>0 from 'R contains non-inquiry payload' to the more precise 'R contains variation not determined by Q,' explicitly noting this Q-extraneous variation may still be valuable for provenance, auditability, explainability, or answering a different future inquiry -- so H(R|Q)=0 means 'no Q-extraneous variation,' not 'nothing else is useful.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: A: Is R sufficient? <-> N_viol, H_hat(Q|R). B: Does O realize the contract? <-> A(R), F(R). C: How much Q-extraneous representation remains? <-> H_hat(R|Q). D: Where does reduction cross the boundary? <-> n*.
a_rows_sample.statement: Freezes a four-question decomposition of the KR-REP-REDUCTION protocol (sufficiency, contract realization, excess representation, boundary) each matched to a specific empirical observable (N_viol/H_hat(Q|R); A(R)/F(R); H_hat(R|Q); n*), and separates three independently-diagnosable boundary-failure kinds (Representation Boundary: N_viol>0 or H(Q|R)>0; Contract Boundary: A(R)<1; Operator Boundary: H(Q|R)=0 but F(R)<1), noting 'information was lost != contract was violated != decoder was inadequate' as three genuinely different failure modes that a reduction can exhibit.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A two-state representation can have entropy close to 1 bit, while a larger representation can have much lower entropy if its distribution is highly concentrated. ... distinguish representation capacity, storage cost, Shannon entropy, minimality.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects a proposed requirement of strictly decreasing entropy H(R_n)<H(R_{n+1}) across the reduction chain as too strong, since entropy depends on the induced probability distribution rather than representation size; recommends requiring strictly decreasing representation CAPACITY instead, and measuring entropy, storage cost, and minimality as independent, separately reported quantities.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A failed representation transition Rn -> Rn-1 demonstrates that the transformation does not preserve the contract for that sample. It does not automatically identify a unique payload S that was removed.
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns against over-interpreting a failed reduction step: multiple eliminated components, interaction effects, transformation-induced changes, recombination, or loss of relational structure could all produce the same observed failure, so a specific eliminated set S notin Elim_{T,Pi}(D) may only be inferred when T_n has an explicit, declared elimination decomposition T_n=E_{S_n} -- otherwise report only 'T_n crosses the preservation boundary for D_i,' connecting this directly to the KR-ZERO-ORDER finding that transformation loss should not be assumed to decompose element-wise.

a_rows_sample.anchor: H(T)=H(Q)+H(T|Q), therefore H(T)>=H(Q), with equality iff H(T|Q)=0 ... T(D) = G(Q(D)) almost surely ... T(D) and Q(D) are mutually deterministically recoverable almost surely.
a_rows_sample.statement: Confirms Theorem 3's corrected attainability condition H(T(D)|Q(D))=0 and its consequence H(T)=H(Q)+H(T|Q); corrects the proposed 'Level 4: Q-Isomorphic Representation' (from Q=O∘T alone) to 'Q-Equivalent Representation,' since factorization through T establishes only that T contains enough information to determine Q, not a bijection between the full codomains Y and Q-space; the stronger, correct claim requires both H(Q(D)|T(D))=0 and H(T(D)|Q(D))=0, giving mutual a.s. recoverability T(D) <-> Q(D) rather than an unproven isomorphism.

a_rows_sample.anchor: sim_{Pi,T} = sim_Q restricted to X_{Pi,T} ... T(D) cannot literally be an element of [D]_{sim_Pi} ... D sim_{Pi,T} E_S(D) because Q(D)=Q(E_S(D)).
a_rows_sample.statement: Repairs two structural errors: (1) the equivalence relation sim_Pi must be defined as the global Q-induced relation sim_Q restricted to the T-dependent admissible domain X_{Pi,T}, not as an independent relation whose domain and defining condition are conflated; (2) a 'same fiber' claim mixing source-space [D]_{sim_Pi} (subset of X) with representation-space elements T(D), T(E_S(D)) (elements of Y) is type-incorrect -- the correct statement is D sim_{Pi,T} E_S(D) in source space, with O(T(D))=O(T(E_S(D))) as the separate representation-space consequence.

a_rows_sample.anchor: T_Adeq(Q) = {T: H(Q(D)|T(D))=0} ... T_Real(Pi) = {T: P(D in X_{Pi,T})=1 and P(O(T(D))=Q(D))=1}.
a_rows_sample.statement: Separates a previously ambiguous family T_adequate(Pi) into two explicitly distinct families -- T_Adeq(Q) (transformations adequate for the inquiry alone) and T_Real(Pi) (transformations that additionally realize the whole contract, both admissibility and the fixed decoder) -- and cautions that entropy minimization T*=argmin H(T(D)) should be stated as an infimum unless existence of the minimizer is separately established.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Zero_{T_n,Pi}(S_n;R^n) => Adeq(R^{n-1},Q,Pi) as the Zero-boundary hypothesis. I would not formulate it that strongly anymore ... Zero is itself a judgment produced by (D,T,Pi,S).
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects a proposed strong 'Zero-boundary hypothesis' (Zero at a reduction step implies adequacy of the next representation) as formulated too strongly, arguing instead that Zero is one observable judgment produced by the underlying tuple (D,T,Pi,S), with an unnamed interaction structure I_{T,Pi}(D,S) as the real open mathematical object -- reframing the research question from 'what does Zero predict?' to 'what structure determines the boundary at which reduction ceases to preserve the contract, of which Zero is one detection mechanism?'

a_rows_sample.anchor: KR-ZERO discovered empirical constraints on context-dependent eliminability and revealed that relational structure may enter through the transformation/preservation pair. KR-REP-REDUCTION now independently investigates representation reduction ... using the KR-ZERO findings as controlled experimental factors and hypotheses -- not as definitions or conclusions.
a_rows_sample.statement: Revises the relationship between the two experiment families: rather than 'KR-ZERO discovers eliminability; KR-REP-REDUCTION tests whether Zero predicts adequacy,' the corrected position is that KR-ZERO's findings become controlled experimental factors and hypotheses for KR-REP-REDUCTION, never definitions or conclusions it inherits; elevates the representation carrier (individual element vs subset vs relational structure/hypergraph/rewriting state) to a first-class unresolved research question that must be settled before R5->R2 can be properly designed.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Adequacy != Contract Realization ... otherwise a representation could look mathematically sufficient while failing the actual preservation/operational contract.
a_rows_sample.statement: Adopts Adequacy != Contract Realization as a hard experimental rule for KR-REP-REDUCTION, distinguishing T_Adeq(Q) (sufficient information exists) from T_Real(Pi) (the specified operator O actually realizes it, and admissibility holds), so that a mathematically sufficient representation is never conflated with one that actually satisfies the operational contract.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KR-ZERO: When can source material be eliminated while preserving the contract? KR-REP-REDUCTION: How far can the representation be reduced while retaining inquiry adequacy and contract realization? The bridge is a hypothesis to test, not an established implication.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the final, precise research-question separation between the two experiment families and explicitly classifies the connecting arrow (Zero_{T_n,Pi} -> candidate elimination -> R^{n-1} -> Adequacy/Realization) as a hypothesis to be tested by KR-REP-REDUCTION, never an established implication inherited from KR-ZERO; freezes a status ledger distinguishing [CORPUS] established facts, [EXP] established mathematical results (H(Q|T)=0 adequacy; H(T|Q)=0 no-excess; hence H(T)=H(Q)+H(T|Q)), [PROP] proposed measures (Excess_Q(T)=H(T|Q); Zero predicting adequacy), and five explicit [OPEN] questions (existence of a general R5->R2 chain; the representation carrier; monotonicity; whether Zero predicts the boundary; whether relational structure in T,Pi predicts reduction difficulty).

a_rows_sample.anchor: X_Q(R) = H(R|Q) as Q-relative residual representation, with excess representation as an interpretation only when the contract explicitly says those distinctions are unnecessary.
a_rows_sample.statement: Names the final residual-representation quantity X_Q(R)=H(R|Q) as 'Q-relative residual representation,' explicitly reserving the normatively loaded term 'excess representation' only for cases where the preservation contract itself declares the residual distinctions unnecessary, on the principle that what is unnecessary for one inquiry is not thereby unnecessary for every inquiry (provenance, uncertainty bounds, or lineage may be irrelevant to Q while still required by the broader contract Pi).

a_rows_sample.anchor: R(Q,Pi) = (D, {R_n}, {T_n}, O, Q, Pi) ... M_n = (A_n, F_n, H_hat(Q|R_n), X_Q(R_n), H_hat(R_n), N_viol,n) ... n* = min{n in {1..5} : Comp_n=1.0 and A_n=1.0 and N_viol,n=0 and H_hat(Q|R_n)=0}.
a_rows_sample.statement: Presents the fully frozen KR-REP-REDUCTION experimental protocol as the object R(Q,Pi)=(D,{R_n},{T_n},O,Q,Pi) with directional chain D->T5->R5->T4->R4->T3->R3->T2->R2->T1->R1, entropy/size/count recorded independently per level (monotonicity treated as an empirical hypothesis, never assumed), a completeness-declared per-level measurement vector M_n=(A_n,F_n,H_hat(Q|R_n),X_Q(R_n),H_hat(R_n),N_viol,n), the closed-form fiber-violation formula N_viol,n=sum_r [(sum_q c_{r,q})^2 - sum_q c_{r,q}^2]/2, and the boundary definition n*=min{n: Comp_n=1, A_n=1, N_viol,n=0, H_hat(Q|R_n)=0}, with R_{n*} confirmed as the chain-specific preservation boundary only if the next-lower level fails at least one of those conditions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The current design does not yet fully test H-RR3 (T-Pi interaction) ... the controlled 2x2 experiment is deferred ... the next useful review is of the actual implementation and its FT-1...FT-7 execution results.
a_rows_sample.statement: Notes that the frozen protocol design defers the controlled 2x2 (T_extreme/realistic x Pi_extreme/realistic) test of transformation-preservation interaction (hypothesis H-RR3), so the design phase can investigate the reduction boundary and observe an association with Zero but cannot yet establish a general T-Pi interaction law; records that the theoretical/protocol design phase is complete and the next required review step is of the actual implementation's FT-1 through FT-7 execution results, i.e. an experiment run beyond the scope of this file.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Contract failure: NO / Operator-only failure: NO / Representation failure: YES ... A_n = 1.000 at every level ... You need a representation where H(Q|R)=0 while simultaneously O(R)!=Q.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reports that hypothesis H-B (intending to separate representation failure, contract failure, and operator failure) found only representation failure occurring, since admissibility A_n=1.000 held at every level and the fixed decoder F=1.000 at the only adequate level R5, so no empirical state arose where Q was recoverable from R (H(Q|R)=0) yet the fixed operator O failed to recover Q (O(R)!=Q); concludes that a fixed decoder alone does not create an operator-boundary experiment -- a representation must retain enough information (H(Q|R)=0) while the chosen decoder still fails to use it -- and this chain never produced such a state, so adequacy and realization remain conceptually distinct even though this experiment did not empirically separate them along the reduction chain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ascending: F_argmax = 0.8667 / descending: F_argmax = 0.3230 ... a difference of 54.37 percentage points ... yet H(Q|R2) 3.3937 vs 3.3965 is essentially unchanged.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reports a strong empirical demonstration that representation adequacy is distinct from fixed-decoder realization: reversing a rank encoding convention (ascending vs descending) leaves Hhat(Q|R2) essentially unchanged (3.3937 vs 3.3965) and N_viol similar, yet the fixed decoder's F_argmax swings by 54.37 percentage points (0.8667 vs 0.3230); interprets this as same recoverable information under different encoding convention producing very different fixed-decoder performance, i.e. a representation can preserve the same recoverable information while a particular fixed decoder performs very differently because it interprets the representation differently.

a_rows_sample.anchor: "A change carrying NO information about D..." ... The ascending and descending rank conventions are information-equivalent recodings of the same rank representation, yet they produce substantially different performance for the fixed decoder O.
a_rows_sample.statement: Requests softening the phrase 'a change carrying no information about D' to the more formal 'the ascending and descending rank conventions are information-equivalent recodings of the same rank representation, yet they produce substantially different performance for the fixed decoder O', on the ground that what matters theoretically is not an informal claim of 'no information' but that the transformation between conventions is information-preserving/invertible; connects this directly to the project's Q-equivalence concept.

a_rows_sample.anchor: bytes: 37 -> 37 -> 37 -> 25 / fields: 2 -> 2 -> 2 -> 2 / cardinality: 26826 -> 5696 -> 3288 -> 162 / entropy: 15.04 -> 12.31 -> 11.10 -> 7.17 ... there is no single obvious scalar called "amount of reduction"
a_rows_sample.statement: Reports the four measured reduction-dimension trajectories (bytes, fields, cardinality, entropy) across R5..R2 and argues the evidence only establishes that no single scalar 'amount of reduction' captures all four dimensions -- i.e. reduction is multidimensional and the measured dimensions do not collapse into one common trajectory -- but four observations along a single chain cannot establish statistical independence, so hypothesis H-D's claim that 'the four dimensions move independently' should be softened to that weaker, corpus-supported statement.

a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes two genuinely different gaps that had previously been conflated: epistemic uncertainty U_t(q_i)=f(p_i) (how certain we are that a given measurement is correct) versus state discrepancy D_t=d(hat-K_t,I_t) (how far the measured state is from the ideal/required state); illustrated by two contrasting cases -- high confidence (p=0.999) with a large discrepancy (meaning we are highly certain the system is wrong) versus moderate confidence (p=0.55) with unknown discrepancy (meaning we don't know whether the system is wrong).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Z_t=0 does not automatically mean Truth=1, because our measurement itself may be uncertain. That preserves the earlier distinction between confidence and authority.
a_rows_sample.statement: Refines Zero(K_t,I_t,E_t) as a distance evaluation Z_t=d(hat-K_t,I_t) with Z_t=0 meaning hat-K_t is equivalent to I_t under the dimensions/metric being evaluated, but explicitly warns Z_t=0 does not thereby entail Truth=1, since the measurement producing hat-K_t may itself be uncertain -- preserving the confidence-vs-authority distinction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Case A — knowledge changes, observation does not ... Case B — observation changes ... Case C — both
a_rows_sample.statement: Resolves the previously repeatedly-raised open question ('does a changed knowledge state mean a changed observation?') into three explicit cases: Case A, O_t=O_{t+1} but K_t!=K_{t+1} (a new dimension was discovered or better evidence obtained, the object itself did not change); Case B, O_t!=O_{t+1} (the actual observed entity changed); Case C, both change simultaneously -- giving a proper temporal model for the identity question the corpus had left explicitly unresolved.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS = KST-compatible state mathematics + epistemic semantics + temporal semantics + provenance + governance
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicitly lists what Knowledge Space Theory does NOT solve for KnowledgeOS (truth, provenance, authority, justification, historical reconstruction, observation identity, institutional knowledge, contextual knowledge, non-monotonic revision, the meaning of an Ideal State, the atomic-knowledge-unit notion itself), rejecting the identification KnowledgeOS=KST in favor of KnowledgeOS = KST-compatible state mathematics + epistemic semantics + temporal semantics + provenance + governance.

a_rows_sample.statement: Reduces the theory's open problems from ten to six named research gaps: G1 precisely defining k_i and its atomicity criterion; G2 defining script-K's mathematical structure (set system? lattice? measurable space? something richer?); G3 defining P(k_i|E_<=t) precisely, distinguishing uncertainty from truth and authority; G4 mathematically defining the Ideal State I_t(O,C,G), called probably the most important remaining gap; G5 defining the distance function Delta_t=d(hat-K_t,I_t), possibly non-Euclidean; G6 defining the transition K_t->K_{t+1} and typing what kind of change (new information, correction, discovery, revision, observation change, or identity change) it represents.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The fundamental object of KnowledgeOS may not be Knowledge... It may be the **epistemic history from which different forms of Knowledge can be reconstructed and evaluated.**
a_rows_sample.statement: Concludes Knowledge is probably not the Kernel's foundational object, and proposes instead that KnowledgeOS's fundamental object is the epistemic history from which different forms of Knowledge can be reconstructed and evaluated; explains this would account for why provenance, time, identity, participant, context, and projections all matter, why Knowledge cannot be equated with probability, why Knowledge Space cannot automatically be equated with a measure space, and why the Kernel should be much smaller than the total KnowledgeOS. Names this the central research hypothesis, explicitly not yet a final architecture, and recommends a seven-area comparative research matrix (Knowledge ontology, epistemic state, Knowledge Space, Knowledge change, historical substrate, Kernel theory, computer-brain architecture) before any Kernel admission.

a_rows_sample.anchor: there is already a legitimate mathematical meaning of Knowledge Space
a_rows_sample.statement: Doignon and Falmagne's Knowledge Space Theory defines a domain Q of knowledge items and a collection of possible knowledge states K, giving (Q,K) an established, different mathematical meaning of 'Knowledge Space' than KnowledgeOS's broader intended sense (which asks how a computational system preserves, evolves, reconstructs and operates over knowledge-bearing states, evidence, participants, context and derived epistemic results, not merely which knowledge states are possible for an individual in a domain); recommends treating 'Knowledge Space' as a contested/established term requiring explicit disambiguation rather than renaming the KnowledgeOS concept.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Remove(X) ⇒ fundamental KnowledgeOS guarantee fails
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a microkernel-derived (seL4-style minimal trusted computing base) Kernel admission test: Remove(X) implies a fundamental KnowledgeOS guarantee fails, replacing the weaker test 'X is useful implies X belongs in the Kernel'. Applying it narrows Kernel candidates to Identity, History, Provenance, Context, Temporal Integrity, and Reconstruction as strong candidates -- explicitly smaller than the earlier 10-12-object Kernel models -- while classifying Justification, Authority, and Consistency as probably not universal/needing qualification, and Truth, Probability, Measurement, Reasoning, and LLM intelligence as external to the Kernel. Also distinguishes SubstrateIdentity, PropositionalIdentity, and EpistemicStateIdentity as three identities that may need separation, since a Knowledge object receiving new evidence could be same-identity-changed-state, a new epistemic object, a version/revision, or a new projection of the same substrate.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Jean-Paul Doignon & Jean-Claude Falmagne — Knowledge Spaces. This is probably the single most important mathematical book for our Knowledge Space question.
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies Doignon & Falmagne's Knowledge Spaces as probably the single most important mathematical book for the Knowledge Space question, developing a mathematical theory generalizing partially ordered sets and connecting it to knowledge assessment and stochastic/combinatorial models; proposes investigating whether K (Knowledge Space) is a set of propositions, a set of possible knowledge states, a partially ordered structure, a family of admissible states, a stochastic structure, or something else, and explicitly warns not to assume KnowledgeOS's Knowledge Space is the same as Knowledge Space Theory's — 'compare them.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Substrate → Epistemic Reconstruction → Knowledge Attribution ... The substrate might preserve: who, what, when, source, observation, method, context, provenance, history, access
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes explicitly modeling Substrate -> Epistemic Reconstruction -> Knowledge Attribution, where the substrate preserves who/what/when/source/observation/method/context/provenance/history/access, and a particular epistemological regime then asks 'does this qualify as Knowledge?' (one regime evaluating Truth+Belief+Safety+Ability, another using a different criterion) — described as exactly what regime separation buys.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Can knowledge at time t be reconstructed without storing "knowledge" itself? If yes, that is a profound architectural result.
a_rows_sample.statement: Poses, extending Pritchard's memory discussion, whether knowledge at time t can be reconstructed without storing 'knowledge' itself, calling a positive answer a profound architectural result.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KST does not establish that the Kernel substrate should literally be Q. That is an architectural hypothesis introduced by the analysis, not a result of KST.
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns that Domain -> State Projection, while aligned with the emerging Substrate --Regime--> Projection architecture, is not itself a KST result: KST does not establish that the Kernel substrate should literally be Q; that mapping is an architectural hypothesis introduced by the analysis, not derived from KST.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Model the Kernel as Q and the immutable historical record. ... No. KST defines Q as the domain of items/questions. It does not establish: Kernel=Q. That's an architectural mapping invented by the analysis.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicitly rejects three claims from the source analysis as not carried forward as facts: (1) 'model the Kernel as Q and the immutable historical record' — Kernel=Q is an invented architectural mapping, not a KST result; (2) 'Knowledge State is a perfect candidate for Projection' — downgraded to a candidate, not perfect, since KST's state has a specific person-can-solve interpretation requiring testing against other epistemic phenomena; (3) 'Knowledge Spaces provides a complete framework for KnowledgeOS' — rejected, since KST is rigorous only for one class of knowledge-state-modelling problems and does not address truth, testimony, belief, epistemic justification, temporal truth, institutional knowledge, provenance, understanding, observer dependence, general epistemic state, or AI knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Given a Knowledge Space K, a historical substrate H_{\leq t}, a participant A, and observations O_{\leq t}^A, what mathematical operation produces the participant's epistemic state K_t^A? ... HISTORICAL SUBSTRATE → OBSERVATIONS → EPISTEMIC STATE → {KNOWLEDGE SPACE, PROBABILITY} → EPISTEMIC REGIME → KNOWLEDGE CLAIM → UNDERSTANDING
a_rows_sample.statement: Poses the sharpened next research question: given a Knowledge Space K, historical substrate H_{<=t}, participant A, and observations O_{<=t}^A, what operation produces K_t^A ∈ K (with P(K_t^A=K|O_{<=t}^A) under uncertainty), and only afterward does Pritchard's question apply (K_t^A --R_epistemology--> Knows(A,p)?); proposes a layered research model Historical Substrate -> Observations -> Epistemic State -> {Knowledge Space, Probability} -> Epistemic Regime -> Knowledge Claim -> Understanding, explicitly not yet called the KnowledgeOS architecture, with the next research step attacking the knowledge-space/epistemic-state/knowledge-attribution distinction rather than adding more components.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_{t_1}: "System uses architecture A" ... The old state should not simply disappear. We need: History(K_{≤t}) ... What was known at t1? That is a fundamentally different question from: What is known now?
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues for retaining a full trajectory K_{t0}->K_{t1}->K_{t2}->... rather than only the latest snapshot, illustrated by an architecture-A-to-architecture-B migration example: without History(K_{<=t}), the system cannot answer 'what was known at t1?', a fundamentally different question from 'what is known now?' — supporting the historical-reconstruction hypothesis.

a_rows_sample.anchor: REALITY / DOMAIN → OBSERVATIONS → INFORMATION / EVIDENCE → EPISTEMIC STATE → KNOWLEDGE → KNOWLEDGE TRAJECTORY → KNOWLEDGE SPACE → WHAT CHARACTERISTICS DEFINE IT? → WHAT IS THE MINIMAL SUFFICIENT REPRESENTATION? → KNOWLEDGE UNIT → KERNEL ... that last transition is the one we have not solved yet.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a ten-stage research order rejecting the shortcut Knowledge->Knowledge Entity->Knowledge Kernel: Reality/Domain -> Observations -> Information/Evidence -> Epistemic State -> Knowledge -> Knowledge Trajectory -> Knowledge Space -> 'what characteristics define it?' -> 'what is the minimal sufficient representation?' -> Knowledge Unit -> Kernel; explicitly marks the last transition (Knowledge Unit -> Kernel) as unsolved, and states that KST, Pritchard, and the Chinese-philosophical research together 'tell us exactly what the Kernel definition must eventually explain,' rather than providing a premature Kernel design.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Remove(X) ⇒ Can the relevant Knowledge characteristic still be reconstructed? ... Can X itself be reconstructed from other preserved information? ... Necessary for computation ≠ Necessary for storage.
a_rows_sample.statement: States a minimality admission test for candidate Kernel properties X: Remove(X) => can the relevant Knowledge characteristic still be reconstructed? If yes, X may not belong in the minimal substrate; if no, X becomes a candidate; adds a stronger follow-up question, can X itself be reconstructed from other preserved information?, and the underlying principle Necessary-for-computation ≠ Necessary-for-storage, proposed as potentially yielding a mathematically defensible Kernel admission test.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DOMAIN / REALITY → OBSERVATIONS → INFORMATION / EVIDENCE → {logical regime, probabilistic regime} → EPISTEMIC STATE → KNOWLEDGE CRITERIA → KNOWLEDGE → {current state, historical state} → KNOWLEDGE TRAJECTORY → RECONSTRUCTION → KERNEL QUESTION → What must minimally be preserved?
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives a consolidated flow diagram synthesizing the day's research: Domain/Reality -> Observations -> Information/Evidence -> {logical regime, probabilistic regime P(S_t|I_{<=t})} -> Epistemic State -> Knowledge Criteria -> Knowledge -> {current state, historical state} -> Knowledge Trajectory -> Reconstruction -> Kernel Question ('what must minimally be preserved?'), explicitly labeled a research model, not yet the KnowledgeOS architecture.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The Kernel might preserve a richer substrate (observations, provenance, context, justification) from which different regimes project different decompositions. Overlap in KST might correspond to the fact that different regimes produce different decompositions of the same substrate.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the single most important unanswered question from the KST fact-check as the relationship between KST's structural overlap (equivalent items, shared skills, multiple representations) and epistemic ambiguity in KnowledgeOS (observations not cleanly distinguishing elements); proposes as a research hypothesis (explicitly not established) that the Kernel might preserve a richer substrate (observations, provenance, context, justification) from which different regimes project different decompositions, with overlap in KST corresponding to different regimes producing different decompositions of the same substrate, and probability being one but not the only mechanism for resolving ambiguity.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge extraction ... from: Knowledge storage ... the Kernel may need to preserve the evidence and history from which the extraction can be reconstructed. ... If we only store: "Nexus runs version 3.69" we lose how that conclusion was reached.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Knowledge extraction (may be probabilistic, AI-based, logical, statistical, human-assisted) from Knowledge storage: the Kernel may need to preserve the evidence and history from which extraction can be reconstructed, rather than only the extracted conclusion — illustrated by storing only 'Nexus runs version 3.69' losing how that conclusion was reached, versus preserving underlying information/relationships enabling later reconstruction of estimated-K_t; flagged as a strong argument for provenance and temporal history, though which parts are indispensable still needs proof.

a_rows_sample.anchor: What information must the Kernel preserve so that Knowledge extraction can be repeated, challenged, revised, and reconstructed?
a_rows_sample.statement: Concludes the next major research step is to study the mathematical properties of the extraction function E: I_{<=t} -> estimated-K_t (uncertainty, inference, approximation, revision, convergence/non-convergence, temporal change) rather than designing Kernel entities directly, in order to sharpen the Kernel question into: what information must the Kernel preserve so that Knowledge extraction can be repeated, challenged, revised, and reconstructed?

a_rows_sample.anchor: We try our best, but because the available information is incomplete and the phenomenon is complex, the extracted Knowledge is an approximation. ... Under what conditions does K̂_t → K_t^*? And perhaps more importantly: Under what conditions can it never converge?
a_rows_sample.statement: States that the Gauss-approximation insight should be central to the research and not merely a footnote, and poses two paired research questions: under what conditions does the extracted estimate estimated-K_t converge to the ideal K_t*, and, more importantly, under what conditions can it never converge — identified as where probability, statistics, inverse problems, estimation theory, and epistemology become genuinely interesting together.

a_rows_sample.anchor: documentation can act as a carrier of justification, but the document itself is not necessarily the justification. ... Document → Evidence/Decision/Rule/Provenance. ... The Kernel may need to preserve the justification relationship, not simply "a document."
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes documentation (which can record what happened, what was decided, why, which rule applied, who authorized it, which evidence supported it) as a carrier of justification, not the justification itself; argues the Kernel may need to preserve the justification relationship (Document -> Evidence/Decision/Rule/Provenance), not merely 'a document.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knows(a, p, c, t) ... Factivity contract (semantic, not a generic probability formula): Knows(a,p,c,t) => Truth(p,c,t). ... Do not replace it with "probability > threshold" or "confidence is high."
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes Knowledge attribution as Knows(a,p,c,t) -- participant a knows proposition/content p in context c at time t -- governed by a factivity contract Knows(a,p,c,t) => Truth(p,c,t), interpreted semantically in the appropriate context; explicitly forbids replacing this factivity contract with 'probability > threshold' or 'confidence is high'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KST shows that the same knowledge structure can be represented in multiple equivalent ways: Family of sets K, Surmise system sigma, Entailment P, Skill map tau. Galois Connections (Chapter 6) ... The invariant is the knowledge structure itself.
a_rows_sample.statement: KST shows the same knowledge structure can be represented in multiple formally equivalent ways (family of feasible states K, surmise system sigma, entailment relation P, skill map tau), related by order-reversing Galois connections; the invariant is the knowledge structure itself -- the set of feasible states K, the domain Q, and the closure properties (for knowledge spaces) -- and the representations are equivalent because they all determine the same K.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 220537 ... extraction is a temporal epistemic process; correctness != completeness != currentness. ... World Change != Information Change != Knowledge Change -- DERIVED by the non-observing-participant case; flagged 'may be one of the most important conceptual invariants.'
b_rows_sample.statement: File 220537 (22:05:37) establishes that extraction is a temporal epistemic process and that correctness, completeness, and currentness of knowledge are three distinct properties, worked through a Nexus 3.69-to-3.80 example proving Complete(K,t1) does not imply Complete(K,t2); derives World Change != Information Change != Knowledge Change via a non-observing-participant case, flagged by the source itself as possibly one of the most important conceptual invariants of the research; and cautions that a mathematical state change should not automatically be given the semantic label 'learning'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 235855 ... Determination is the missing mathematical object; the proposed "invariants" are not invariants. ... uncertainty representation, conditional structure, combination rule, temporal aspect, conflict handling, ignorance representation are dimensions along which frameworks differ, i.e. common research concerns, not invariants -- PROVEN-style
b_rows_sample.statement: File 235855 (23:58:55), the terminal open question of Day 1, argues that Determination is the missing mathematical object and that the framework's previously-proposed 'invariants' fail the actual definition of invariance: uncertainty representation, conditional structure, combination rule, temporal aspect, conflict handling, and ignorance representation are dimensions along which competing frameworks differ, i.e. shared research concerns, not invariants -- proven-style by directly applying the definition of invariance. Also marks 'common algebraic structure (lattice/measure-theoretic)' as HIGHLY SPECULATIVE, since P(p), a fuzzy measure mu(p), and Acceptable(p) may represent different epistemic properties rather than one object, and proposes a five-step ordering (epistemic object -> determination operation -> what each regime represents -> equivalence conditions -> what survives) that must precede any invariance claim.

# One important architectural correction

I would **not** make Step 284 wait for Steps 285–289.

That would recreate the very category error we have spent Steps 280–283 eliminating.

The Book Architecture Gate can operate with:

$$
FC=TRUE,\quad
CC=	ext{known status},\quad
EC=FALSE,\quad
GC=	ext{known status}
$$
b_rows_sample.statement: Explicit architectural correction: Step 284 (Book Architecture Gate) must not be made to wait for Steps 285-289 (computational/empirical/measurement/governance/end-to-end certification), because doing so would recreate the same category error (conflating theory closure with implementation/empirical/governance completeness) that Steps 280-283 were spent eliminating; the book gate can and should operate with FC=TRUE, CC/GC at whatever their known actual status is, and EC=FALSE, as long as those statuses are stated accurately rather than silently upgraded.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
# STEP 290 — FINAL CERTIFICATION DECISION

Only now should there be another global closure decision.

It should calculate independently:

$$
\mathcal C =
(FC,CC,EC,GC)
$$

and issue one of:

### A — Theory remains open ... ### B — Theory closed, certification incomplete ... ### C — Fully certified
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Step 290 (Final Certification Decision) as the only point at which another global closure decision should occur, computing the 4-tuple C=(FC,CC,EC,GC) independently and choosing among three outcomes: A (theory remains open, only if a genuine theory-critical contradiction or insufficiency is discovered), B (theory closed but certification incomplete, if FC=TRUE while implementation/empirical/governance certification remain incomplete), or C (fully certified, only if all required dimensions are actually evidenced); explicitly preserves the FC!=CC!=EC!=GC rule and forbids inferring EC or GC from FC-and-CC.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ### Philosophical sources may do three things **1. Corroborate** ... **2. Generate a hypothesis** ... **3. Expose a contradiction or blind spot** ... ### They may NOT do four things **1. Define a KnowledgeOS primitive.** **2. Select the canonical vocabulary.** **3. Select the architecture.** **4. Resolve governance.**
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines an explicit boundary for any philosophical-source research programme: sources MAY corroborate an already-independently-derived KnowledgeOS property, generate a hypothesis (suggesting a distinction that might correspond to a missing property), or expose a contradiction/blind spot (highlighting something the existing model cannot represent); sources may NOT define a KnowledgeOS primitive, select the canonical vocabulary, select the architecture, or resolve governance -- those remain internal KnowledgeOS activities.

b_rows_sample.anchor: **The programme now has a second kind of source behaviour.** The Gītā mostly gave you **corroboration and corpus recoveries**. Cavell gives you **potential architectural objections and innovation hypotheses**. ... an objection can open a research question without becoming a primitive, and a philosophical distinction can expose a missing concept without becoming architecture.
b_rows_sample.statement: Identifies the programme's most important meta-conclusion beyond any individual finding: it now has two distinct kinds of philosophical-source behavior -- the Gita mostly produced corroboration and corpus recoveries, while Cavell produces potential architectural objections and innovation hypotheses; this justifies making the research step source-general, but also raises the stakes of promotion discipline, since an objection can open a research question without becoming a primitive, and a distinction can expose a missing concept without becoming architecture.

a_notations: MAY NOT: define primitive, select vocabulary, select architecture, resolve governance
MAY: corroborate, generate hypothesis, expose blind spot

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'two-kinds-of-philosophical-source-behavior' POSSIBLY relates to 'philosophical-source-programme-may-may-not-boundary' (batch B0051). Note: Meta-observation that the philosophical-source research programme now exhibits two qualitatively different source behaviors: the Gita mostly produced corroboration of independently-derived KnowledgeOS properties and corpus recoveries of already-existing constructs, while Cavell produces a different kind of contribution -- potential architectural objections and genuinely new innovation hypotheses the corpus does not already contain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I read the attached document in full. My assessment is that it is useful, but it is not yet safe to merge into the KnowledgeOS theory as written ... The most important work is therefore not to add all 10 proposed distinctions. It is to extract the valid theoretical contribution, correct the formalism, and prevent R_req from becoming an over-constraining 'master ontology.'
a_rows_sample.statement: Executive verdict on an R_req/ratification-style document: classified as research analysis / candidate specification, not yet ratifiable; explicitly rejects the document's own recommendation to add all ten proposed distinctions and to ratify, warning against R_req becoming an over-constraining 'master ontology'; distills the strongest contribution as R_req = the distinctions that must remain available for KnowledgeOS's required questions, combined with Representation Adequacy iff required distinctions are preserved.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the stronger KnowledgeOS definition should be: Adequacy(R,Q,Gamma) iff R preserves all distinctions in D_Q(Gamma) ... not: R preserves every distinction in D. The document itself notices this problem under projection adequacy, where it recommends allowing lower-tier distinctions to be lost. That observation should actually be moved up into the fundamental definition.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the pairwise-preservation definition of adequacy (d(x)!=d(y) implies R(x)!=R(y) for all d) to be question-relative from the start: Adequacy(R,Q,Gamma) iff R preserves all distinctions in D_Q(Gamma), not all distinctions in D universally -- because a representation may legitimately collapse a distinction irrelevant to the current question; promotes an observation the original document made only under 'projection adequacy' up into the foundational definition.

type_signature.domain: representation R, question Q, context Gamma

a_rows_sample.anchor: For KnowledgeOS: Required != Interesting != Available in literature. A distinction belongs in R_req only if we can establish that some KnowledgeOS question, invariant, operation, assurance requirement or boundary requires it. ... analytic/synthetic, a priori/a posteriori, necessary/contingent, intentional/extensional, de dicto/de re ... their existence in the KR/philosophy literature does not establish that KnowledgeOS must preserve them.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the principle Required != Interesting != Available-in-literature: a distinction enters R_req only if some KnowledgeOS question, invariant, operation, assurance requirement, or boundary can be shown to require it; existence in KR/philosophy literature alone (cited for analytic/synthetic, a priori/a posteriori, necessary/contingent, intensional/extensional, de dicto/de re) is not sufficient grounds.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A. Strong candidates: 1. Truth vs. validity ... 2. Satisfiability vs. unsatisfiability ... 3. Soundness vs. completeness ... 4. Decidability vs. undecidability ... 5. Local vs. global scope ... 6. Intensional vs. extensional ... 7. De dicto vs. de re ... B. Probably outside core R_req: Analytic vs. synthetic ... A priori vs. a posteriori ... Necessary vs. contingent ... These should remain external research candidates, not Tier 2 requirements.
a_rows_sample.statement: Splits the document's ten proposed additional distinctions into Group A (strong candidates deserving further KnowledgeOS work: truth-vs-validity, satisfiability-vs-unsatisfiability, soundness-vs-completeness, decidability-vs-undecidability, local-vs-global scope, intensional-vs-extensional, de-dicto-vs-de-re) and Group B (probably outside core R_req: analytic-vs-synthetic, a-priori-vs-a-posteriori, necessary-vs-contingent), recommending Group B remain external research candidates rather than Tier 2 requirements.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Truth vs. Validity -- |=alpha vs. Sigma|=alpha. This is not a clean distinction ... So the important distinction is: Validity != Entailment rather than: Truth != Validity. At the semantic level: M|=alpha is truth of alpha in a model M. Then |=alpha is validity across all models. And Sigma|=alpha is entailment from Sigma. This should be corrected before incorporating the item.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects a formal error in the source document's Truth-vs-Validity distinction: the real three-way distinction is M|=alpha (truth of alpha in model M) versus |=alpha (validity: true in every model) versus Sigma|=alpha (entailment from Sigma); the document's proposed 'Truth vs Validity' pairing is not clean and should be replaced by Validity != Entailment before incorporation.

type_signature.domain: formula alpha, model M, theory Sigma

a_rows_sample.anchor: we already have a critical KnowledgeOS boundary: Satisfiability != Contr because satisfiability is relative to Semantics + Language + ModelClass. Thus: Cons_S(K) iff exists M, M |=_S K could be a candidate formal consistency property. But it must not become: Contr(K) = not Cons_S(K). ... The attached document itself later says Contr requires Support Status and Resolution Status. That is actually evidence against identifying Contr with ordinary satisfiability.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects identifying Contr with ordinary model-theoretic satisfiability: Satisfiability != Contr, since satisfiability is relative to Semantics+Language+ModelClass; proposes Cons_S(K) iff exists M: M|=_S K as a candidate formal consistency property distinct from Contr(K)=not-Cons_S(K), citing the source document's own admission that Contr requires Support Status and Resolution Status as evidence against the satisfiability identification, and listing Contr's broader required distinctions (genuine contradiction, incompatible contexts, temporal divergence, supersession, insufficient evidence, theory incompleteness).

type_signature.domain: knowledge base K under reasoning system S

a_rows_sample.anchor: soundness and completeness are properties of a reasoning system: Sound(S), Complete(S,Q). They are not properties of Knowledge itself. This should therefore be added under: Formal Representation and Reasoning rather than as a universal epistemic distinction. ... Decidability is a property of a problem/procedure/formal system ... Decidable(S,Q) ... Therefore: Decidability != EpistemicStatus. But it is extremely valuable as a reasoning-system capability/property. This fits our existing Complexity(S,Q) work.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reclassifies Soundness (Sound(S)), Completeness (Complete(S,Q)), and Decidability (Decidable(S,Q)) as properties of the reasoning system S (a problem/procedure/formal-system property), not properties of Knowledge itself and not epistemic distinctions (Decidability != EpistemicStatus, distinct from Known(p) and Determined(p)); recommends filing them under 'Formal Representation and Reasoning' alongside an existing Complexity(S,Q) line of work rather than as universal epistemic distinctions in R_req.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The document identifies a weakness in its own preservation criterion: it does not account for context-sensitivity. This is correct. I would make the correction stronger. Instead of D_Q we should eventually have D_Q(Gamma) ... R_req may be a global baseline, while the actual required distinction set is: R_req(Q,Gamma). This is a major improvement.
a_rows_sample.statement: Strengthens the source document's own context-sensitivity self-correction: replaces D_Q with D_Q(Gamma) where Gamma bundles context, scope, time, authority, task, and representation regime; correspondingly R_req becomes a global baseline while the actually-applicable set is R_req(Q,Gamma) -- described as a major theoretical improvement over a fixed universal set.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I disagree with 'Tier 1 must always be preserved' ... A Tier-1 distinction d3 could be irrelevant to that question. Then R_1 may legitimately discard d3. So Tier(d) should influence governance priority, but should not automatically determine semantic preservation. The better rule is: Requiredness(Q,Gamma) > Tier.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects the rule 'Tier 1 must always be preserved' as too rigid: even a Tier-1 distinction may be legitimately discarded by a representation used only for a task whose D_Q does not require it. Proposes Tier should govern governance priority, not automatically determine semantic preservation, i.e. Requiredness(Q,Gamma) takes precedence over Tier.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The document says transformation invariance should preserve distinctions, but then recognizes that transformations may intentionally modify distinctions ... define a transformation's declared change set: Chg(T) subseteq R. Then: d not-in Chg(T) implies T must preserve d. This is much better for KnowledgeOS because some operations are supposed to change state. Otherwise the preservation requirement makes state transition impossible.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the transformation-invariance rule: instead of requiring T to preserve all of R_req, defines a declared change set Chg(T) subseteq R such that d not-in Chg(T) implies T must preserve d; explicitly noting that an unconditional preservation requirement would make state transition impossible, since some operations are supposed to change state.

type_signature.domain: transformation T and distinction set R
type_signature.codomain: Chg(T) subseteq R, plus a preservation obligation on R minus Chg(T)

a_rows_sample.anchor: The document says: delta must preserve all R_req distinctions. I would explicitly reject this formulation ... What must be preserved are the invariants declared applicable to that transition. So: InvariantCustody(delta) is preferable to: PreserveAll(delta, R_req). This aligns directly with our existing invariant-custody research.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicitly rejects the claim 'delta must preserve all R_req distinctions': a transition delta(K_t,a)->K_{t+1} may intentionally change status, support, currency, resolution, scope, even representation; proposes InvariantCustody(delta) -- preserving only the invariants declared applicable to that specific transition -- as preferable to PreserveAll(delta,R_req), aligned with existing invariant-custody research.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 'Zero requires all Tier 1 distinctions' should NOT be adopted ... Zero does not necessarily need every distinction in R_req. Instead: Zero(K,I,Gamma,L) asks what is not justified by the available representation within the declared inquiry boundary. Therefore Zero's required distinctions are: R_Zero(I,Gamma,L) not automatically all Tier-1 distinctions. This is a major correction.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects the claim 'Zero requires all Tier 1 distinctions': Zero(K,I,Gamma,L) does not need every R_req distinction, only R_Zero(I,Gamma,L), a distinct inquiry-relative subset; supports this by restating Zero's own existing epistemic-boundary vocabulary (Unknown!=Absent, NoEvidence!=EvidenceOfAbsence, Unresolved!=False, Representation!=Reality) as the actual grounding, rather than an automatic Tier-1 requirement.

type_signature.domain: inquiry I, context Gamma, lens L

a_rows_sample.anchor: The 'minimality' definition is not yet mathematically sufficient ... minimal relative to what? ... the empty set R=empty could trivially satisfy many formal preservation conditions. The correct direction is something like: R_req(Q,Gamma) = minimal distinctions sufficient for all required questions Q, subject to declared adequacy criteria. This makes R_req task-grounded rather than literature-grounded.
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies a mathematical gap in the source document's minimality claim (a set claimed minimal 'relative to what?' -- as stated, an empty distinction set could trivially satisfy preservation/non-collapse/compositionality conditions); corrects the definition to R_req(Q,Gamma) = the minimal distinction set sufficient for all required questions Q, subject to declared adequacy criteria, making R_req task-grounded rather than literature-grounded.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 'Completeness of R_req' is itself a dangerous concept ... There may be no useful universal set D_all. There can always be another task requiring another distinction. So instead of asking 'Is R_req complete?' we should ask: Complete relative to which task/question/domain? ... Complete(R_req,Q,Gamma) could mean: no currently declared required question in Q requires a distinction absent from R_req. That is a tractable governance question. 'Complete for all possible knowledge representation' is not.
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns that asking whether R_req is 'complete' in an absolute sense is a dangerous, likely-unanswerable question (no useful universal distinction set D_all can be assumed to exist, since any new task can require a new distinction); replaces it with a tractable relativized governance question Complete(R_req,Q,Gamma): no currently declared required question in Q requires a distinction absent from R_req.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The 47 distinctions should therefore NOT be frozen as universal ... Better: 47 currently identified candidate distinctions within the present KnowledgeOS research scope. ... We should preserve KnownSet(R) without claiming R=D.
a_rows_sample.statement: Downgrades the source document's claim that its 47 distinctions form a comprehensive foundation, to '47 currently identified candidate distinctions within the present KnowledgeOS research scope', distinguishing the known distinction set KnownSet(R) from a claim that R equals the (unknowable) universal distinction set D.

a_rows_sample.anchor: After filtering the document, I would extract seven concrete contributions. RQ-1 Required Distinction Set R_req(Q,Gamma) PROMOTE TO THEORY CANDIDATE ... RQ-2 Representation Preservation Preserve(R,d) PROMOTE ... RQ-3 Representation Collapse Collapse(R,d) PROMOTE ... RQ-4 Representation Adequacy Adequacy(R,Q,Gamma) PROMOTE ... RQ-5 Contextual Requiredness R_req = f(Q,Gamma) PROMOTE ... RQ-6 Transformation Change Set Chg(T) subseteq R STRONG CANDIDATE ... RQ-7 Formal Reasoning Properties Sound(S), Complete(S,Q), Decidable(S,Q), Complexity(S,Q) PROMOTE AS REASONING-SYSTEM PROPERTIES
a_rows_sample.statement: Lists seven concrete contributions extracted from the filtered document, each with a promotion status: RQ-1 Required Distinction Set R_req(Q,Gamma) (PROMOTE TO THEORY CANDIDATE); RQ-2 Preserve(R,d) (PROMOTE); RQ-3 Collapse(R,d) (PROMOTE); RQ-4 Adequacy(R,Q,Gamma) (PROMOTE); RQ-5 Contextual Requiredness R_req=f(Q,Gamma) (PROMOTE); RQ-6 Transformation Change Set Chg(T) subseteq R (STRONG CANDIDATE); RQ-7 Formal Reasoning Properties Sound(S)/Complete(S,Q)/Decidable(S,Q)/Complexity(S,Q) (PROMOTE AS REASONING-SYSTEM PROPERTIES).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Loss_req(pi,Q,Gamma) = R_req(Q,Gamma) intersect Collapsed(pi). Then: Loss_req = empty is a very strong adequacy condition. This is far more useful than a generic 'information loss' metric. ... FDE preserves some distinctions but collapses others. The relevant question is not 'Does FDE have four values?' It is: Does FDE preserve every distinction in R_req(Q,Gamma)? Our previous experiments already showed that it does not.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Loss_req(pi,Q,Gamma) = R_req(Q,Gamma) intersect Collapsed(pi) as a required-information-loss metric, with Loss_req=empty as a strong adequacy condition, judged more useful than a generic information-loss measure; reframes the earlier FDE-insufficiency finding not as 'does FDE have four values' but as 'does FDE preserve every distinction in R_req(Q,Gamma)', concluding it does not (per prior experiments) -- positioning R_req as the formal language for STATING why a representation is inadequate rather than a prescription of which representation must be used.

type_signature.domain: projection pi, question Q, context Gamma
type_signature.codomain: a subset of R_req(Q,Gamma) that pi collapses

a_rows_sample.anchor: Zero -> Boundary analysis -> Required distinctions rather than: Zero = absence of Tier-1 distinctions. This is a substantial theoretical improvement. ... each operation should have: Pre(delta), Post(delta), Inv(delta), Chg(delta). Then: d in Inv(delta) means the distinction must survive the transition. Whereas: d in Chg(delta) means the transition is explicitly permitted/required to change it. This is much more compatible with DDD and formal transition semantics.
a_rows_sample.statement: Clarifies the role of Zero as Zero->Boundary-analysis->Required-distinctions (not Zero=absence-of-Tier-1-distinctions), and clarifies delta's structure as needing four named components -- Pre(delta), Post(delta), Inv(delta) (distinctions that must survive the transition), and Chg(delta) (distinctions the transition is permitted/required to change) -- judged more compatible with DDD and formal transition semantics than a single undifferentiated preserve-everything rule.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The attached document recommends: HPA review -> feedback -> ratification -> kernel selection. I would change the last step. Do not: R_req -> KernelSelection directly. Instead: R_req -> AdequacyConstraints -> CandidateRepresentations -> CandidateOperations -> Verification -> KernelSelection. This is crucial. R_req tells us what must not be lost. It does not tell us which implementation/formalism is the kernel.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects the source document's governance chain (HPA review -> feedback -> ratification -> kernel selection, with R_req feeding kernel selection directly), replacing the last step with a longer chain: R_req -> AdequacyConstraints -> CandidateRepresentations -> CandidateOperations -> Verification -> KernelSelection; states R_req tells us what must not be lost, not which implementation/formalism is the kernel.

a_rows_sample.statement: Consolidated final classification table judging each part of the reviewed document: most core concepts (R_req, Preservation, Collapse, Adequacy, Projection analysis) rated Strong (some with corrections); Composition preservation rated too strong as written; Tier system rated a useful governance device but not semantic law; several proposed distinctions (analytic/synthetic, a priori/a posteriori, necessary/contingent) rated Not currently required; and five specific claims explicitly Rejected -- Zero=all-Tier-1, Contr=satisfiability-failure, delta-preserves-all-R_req, 47-distinctions=complete, and direct kernel selection -- with immediate ratification rated Premature.

b_rows_sample.anchor: > **What evaluation structure is minimally required to preserve the distinctions the KnowledgeOS programme has already declared important?**
b_rows_sample.statement: W-KR-CONTR-2026-09 reframes the Contr question from 'three vs four values' to the deeper question of what evaluation structure is minimally required to preserve the programme's already-declared-important distinctions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: * Candidate A — fourth value: **7/12** * Candidate B — delegation: **7/12** * Candidate C — exclusive construction: **7/12** * Candidate D — structured evaluation: **12/12**
b_rows_sample.statement: Reports the core scoring result: A/B/C each pass only 7/12 required distinctions, failing on the identical seven; D (structured evaluation) passes all 12. The seven common failures collapse the unknown family (Unobservable≡InsufficientEvidence≡Underdetermined≡TheoryIncomplete≡...→U), meaning adding a contradiction value does not address distinctions lying outside the contradiction dimension.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
$$
\chi(G)=3.
$$... **Given this particular required-distinction set and this adequacy criterion, at least three distinguishable flat classes are required.**
b_rows_sample.statement: The experiment turns adequacy into a graph-coloring/injectivity problem over the required-distinction graph, finding chromatic number chi(G)=3; carefully qualified: this does not establish the correct evaluation domain has three values, only that at least three distinguishable flat classes are required given this distinction set and adequacy criterion -- and separately, nine 'no determinate value' conditions cannot be adequately represented by any flat value domain regardless of cardinality, making the obstruction structural rather than cardinal.

States a methodological principle from the chromatic-number finding: colourability only proves pairwise coding capacity under the chosen abstraction, it does not establish that resulting values carry the required semantic or operational meaning -- cardinality sufficiency is not semantic adequacy.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
$$
\min |\text{representation}|=2
$$

with the two minimum representations: $$
\{\text{value},\text{reason}\}
$$

and $$
\{\text{polarity},\text{reason}\}.
$$

And: **reason is indispensable.**
b_rows_sample.statement: The exhaustive minimum-representation search finds min|representation|=2, with two minimum representations {value,reason} and {polarity,reason}, establishing that reason is indispensable -- evaluation outcome is not value alone, EVal=(v,r) is the minimum representation found in the tested search space, kept explicitly [EXP]/[PROP] not a new KnowledgeOS primitive.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Candidate C maps contradiction to `T`. Yet it passes invariants I1–I5. Why? Because those invariants test contradiction against the **unknown family**, rather than against satisfaction itself.
b_rows_sample.statement: Candidate C (exclusive construction) maps Contradiction to T (Satisfied) yet passes invariants I1-I5, because those invariants only test Contr≠Unknown-family, not Contr≠Satisfied -- exposing a genuine coverage gap in the invariant suite itself, not merely a bad candidate; proposes I11: Contr≠Satisfied as a legitimate but not-yet-ratified [PROP] test-protocol addition, explicitly preserving the historical conflict (I1-I5 pass, capability guard fails) rather than retroactively declaring the suite complete.

b_rows_sample.anchor:

The first implementation unfairly returned `T` for theory-incomplete/uninterpreted cases... ### E7

The literal `"C"` detector accidentally matched context identifiers such as `C1/C2`.
b_rows_sample.statement: Records two implementation self-corrections during the experiment: R_A, an initial implementation unfairly returned T for theory-incomplete/uninterpreted cases, corrected so all nine no-determinate-value conditions return U; E7, a literal 'C' contradiction detector accidentally matched context identifiers like C1/C2, corrected -- both classified as test-implementation defects, not candidate properties, caught by investigating rather than forcing expected results (E9).

b_rows_sample.anchor: > **The experiment does not support representing contradiction as a distinguished scalar evaluation value. b_rows_sample.statement: States the accepted formulation of the current Contr finding: the experiment does not support representing contradiction as a distinguished scalar value; a structured representation with an indispensable reason-like dimension satisfies the tested adequacy requirement; the precise evaluation semantics including contradiction's role remains OPEN -- explicitly weaker and safer than 'structured evaluation is the answer', since D is the surviving candidate, not yet the final theory.

b_rows_sample.statement: Clarifies the role of Zero as Zero->Boundary-analysis->Required-distinctions (not Zero=absence-of-Tier-1-distinctions), and clarifies delta's structure as needing four named components -- Pre(delta), Post(delta), Inv(delta) (distinctions that must survive the transition), and Chg(delta) (distinctions the transition is permitted/required to change) -- judged more compatible with DDD and formal transition semantics than a single undifferentiated preserve-everything rule.
